title: Title: Non-Linear Vector Calculus with Adaptive Kernel Selection
abstract: Vector calculus, a foundational tool in mathematics and physics, has historically been constrained by its inherent linearity. This limitation hinders its application to complex, non-linear systems, where traditional methods struggle to provide accurate results. This paper introduces a novel approach to vector calculus – Non-Linear Vector Calculus with Adaptive Kernel Selection – that addresses this bottleneck by dynamically selecting the most appropriate kernel function for each variable within the calculation. The core mechanism involves learning a mapping between the system's dynamics and the kernel function itself, allowing the algorithm to adapt to the specific problem and system characteristics. This leads to improved accuracy and robustness in handling non-linear systems, offering a significant advancement over existing techniques. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, demonstrates its effectiveness through illustrative examples, and discusses potential future directions.

abstract: The present work introduces a novel high-order group complexity model designed to predict algorithm execution times with improved accuracy and predictability. Traditional complexity analysis often relies on static analysis, limiting its ability to accurately estimate runtime. This model leverages the dynamic properties of high-order groups to provide more precise and insightful complexity estimations. This research focuses on developing a model that adapts to the specific structure of the algorithm being analyzed, leading to a more robust and informative complexity assessment. The core mechanism centers around a refined approach to estimating execution time based on group structure, enabling a significant advancement in computational complexity prediction.

abstract: This paper explores the application of a dynamic probabilistic model to enhance the performance of genetic algorithms. Traditional genetic algorithms often suffer from the limitations of static parameter settings, restricting the search space and hindering optimal solutions. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts the parameters of the probabilistic model during the search process, enabling the algorithm to escape local optima and identify more promising regions of the search space. The core mechanism involves learning a probability distribution that influences the genetic operators, leading to improved search efficiency and higher quality solutions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and experimental analysis, showing significant improvements in convergence speed and solution quality compared to traditional genetic algorithms. title: Quantum Key Distribution Based on Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed key generation scheme based on quantum entanglement, aiming to achieve fully secure key distribution without prior key exchange. The core concept leverages quantum entanglement between two or more nodes to generate and transmit keys, combined with a quantum key distribution protocol for verification and error correction. Unlike existing quantum key distribution schemes reliant on quantum communication channels, this approach offers a theoretically more secure and potentially efficient method for key sharing. The system utilizes Bell states, polarization measurements, and post-processing techniques to establish a shared key. We outline the key components of the system, including entanglement generation, measurement protocols, error correction, and key distillation. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the security of the scheme against eavesdropping attacks, assuming the validity of quantum mechanics. This work contributes to the ongoing research in quantum cryptography and provides a foundational design for a future generation of secure communication networks.

title: Graph-Based Representation Learning for Natural Language Understanding using Relational Embeddings
abstract: This paper investigates the limitations of traditional word embedding techniques in capturing the intricate relational structures inherent in natural language. We propose a novel approach utilizing graph-based representation learning, specifically employing relational embeddings learned through graph convolutional networks (GCNs). The core idea is to represent language as a graph, where nodes represent words and edges represent semantic relationships derived from various sources like syntactic dependencies and co-occurrence patterns. By learning embeddings that encode these relationships, we aim to create a more nuanced and context-aware representation of word meaning. Our approach demonstrates improved performance in downstream natural language understanding tasks compared to conventional word embedding methods. The key innovation lies in the systematic integration of graph structure with embedding learning, providing a richer representation capable of modeling the complex dependencies that define language.

title: Cognitive Graph Embedding for Knowledge Graph Completion
abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) is a crucial task in leveraging the wealth of information stored within knowledge graphs (KGs). Traditional graph embedding methods often treat nodes and edges equally, failing to capture the nuanced relationships and cognitive processes that underpin human understanding of knowledge. This paper proposes a novel cognitive graph embedding framework that integrates attention mechanisms and memory modules to enhance KGC accuracy. The core idea is to model the cognitive aspects of knowledge representation and reasoning by allowing the embedding model to selectively attend to relevant nodes based on their context and retain memories of past interactions. We introduce a new algorithm, Cognitive Graph Embedding (CGE), which incorporates both attention and memory into the embedding process. CGE learns node embeddings that capture both structural information and cognitive biases, resulting in improved performance on KGC benchmarks. The experiments demonstrate that CGE outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with sparse or noisy knowledge graphs. The key contributions of this work are the integration of cognitive principles into graph embedding and the development of a practical algorithm for KGC.

title: Based on Multi-Agent Collaboration for Distributed Robot Control
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to distributed robot control leveraging the power of multi-agent collaboration. Traditional centralized control schemes often struggle with scalability and robustness, particularly in complex environments and dynamic tasks. This research proposes a decentralized control methodology where multiple robots operate autonomously, employing a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework to achieve coordinated task execution. The core innovation lies in the decentralized decision-making process, eliminating the bottleneck of a central controller and enabling robust adaptation to unforeseen circumstances. The system utilizes a distributed MARL algorithm to facilitate communication and cooperation between the robots, allowing them to collectively solve problems that would be intractable for a single robot. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, setting the stage for future experimental validation. ---

title: 自适应量子算法的优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum algorithm optimization centered on dynamically adjusting quantum algorithm parameters. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, which are inadequate for the inherently variable nature of quantum computation, particularly in the context of large-scale quantum systems. We propose a system that leverages a combination of quantum path optimization and adaptive parameter tuning to significantly enhance the efficiency of quantum algorithms. This research focuses on creating a mechanism that can dynamically adjust quantum algorithm parameters based on the current state of the quantum system, leading to improved performance. The core mechanism involves integrating quantum path optimization with a self-adaptive parameter tuning strategy, enabling the algorithm to self-correct and refine its trajectory. The paper details the proposed system's architecture, demonstrates its effectiveness through theoretical analysis, and provides a preliminary evaluation of its capabilities. The objective is to provide a robust and adaptable framework for optimizing quantum algorithms, addressing a key challenge in the field of quantum computing.

abstract: The development of robust and generalizable deep learning models has been a significant challenge in recent years. The core of our work involves a novel error-based and data distribution-aware regularization framework. We evaluate the proposed method on several benchmark RNN tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing model robustness and generalization capabilities.

title: Ensemble clustering: A practical tutorial
abstract: Cluster analysis is an explorative analytical method, serving as a critical tool in psychology, psychiatry, and related fields to map heterogeneous data into meaningful subgroups. Despite their extensive historical use, traditional clustering techniques suffer from a lack of stability, robustness, and generalisability. These issues stem from the inherent difficulties of the clustering optimisation problem as well as the stochastic nature of algorithm optimisers. To address these challenges, we demonstrate the use of methods utilising ensemble learning techniques to combine clustering results from different algorithms, model specifications, and/or sampled sub-datasets to form a single, more reliable consensus of clustering solutions. We detail ensemble clustering principles and variations in base clustering generation models and ensemble methods. More importantly, detailed introductions in existing R libraries and practical examples using R code are provided to guide users in both implementing and optimising ensemble clustering models. As a practical tutorial, we then include simulation studies of real-world data to demonstrate the substantial benefit of ensemble clustering compared with single-run clustering models. The resources presented here will enable researchers to apply advanced clustering techniques to decompose heterogeneous and complex psychological data into stable subgroups.

title: QKD-Assisted Secure Transport Framework for Federated Healthcare Systems: A Software Prototype and Baseline Evaluation
abstract: Decentralised machine learning requires authenticated transport to secure exchanged model updates. To this end, this study presents a healthcare-focused proof of concept integrating a quantum key distribution (QKD) simulation with HKDF-SHA-256, AES-256-GCM, role-based access control, replay detection, and sample-weighted federated averaging (FedAvg), and evaluates it on 42,989 medical records across 1107 synthetic patients. A trusted server decrypted authorised updates before plaintext aggregation. Centralised logistic regression achieved an F1 score of 0.7483, while a five-client FedAvg achieved 0.7333. Encrypted and unencrypted pipelines demonstrated identical model parameters. The simulated QKD protocol produced a mean quantum bit error rate of 0.2486 and successfully aborted all sessions under a full intercept constraint. Under ten independent data splits, the five-client FedAvg achieved mean F1 scores of 0.6973 (IID) and 0.6104 (non-IID). Demonstrating that transport security does not mitigate adversarial machine learning, an authenticated sign-flip attack bypassed AES-256-GCM protection and reduced the mean F1 score to 0.1185. Computationally, the QKD-assisted path averaged 0.386 ms per update compared to 0.486 ms for fresh TLS 1.3 and 0.006 ms for persistent TLS while isolating software execution from hardware constraints. Overall, this study demonstrates a reproducible proof of concept and a practical baseline for a secure machine learning approach for healthcare collaborations.

Overall, this study demonstrates a reproducible proof of concept and a practical baseline for a secure machine learning approach for healthcare collaborations.

title: Enhancing E-commerce Chatbot Design with Customer Journey Mapping: Survey and NLP Analysis of User Inquiries
abstract: Despite adoption of chatbots in e-commerce, chatbots struggle to maintain context, provide complete policy guidance, or respond appropriately to post-purchase problems. This study maps user questions as shoppers’ needs at different points in the Customer Journey Map (CJM). A cross-sectional survey collected users’ opinions on expected chatbot interactions in an e-commerce setting. Sixty participants provided responses on which three questions they would ask an e-commerce chatbot during online shopping. Three unsupervised machine-learning approaches were used: Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling, K -means clustering, and Lexicon-based analysis. We compared themes and clusters from the Lexicon and K -means methods with the topics generated by LDA. Mapping inquiries to the CJM showed the largest share in Consideration (35%), followed by Decision (30%), Awareness (20%), and Post-Purchase (15%). Overall sentiment of inquiries was observed to be predominantly neutral, Awareness questions had a largely positive tone, and Post-Purchase questions had a largely negative tone.

title: Beyond Lie Algebras: Lie-Wedge Stratification and Pure-State Stabilizability in Single-Channel Qubit Control
abstract: Lie algebras describe how control generators combine, but in open systems they erase the distinction between reversible control and irreversible dissipation. Lie wedges retain this information. We study drift-free single-qubit systems with bidirectional Hamiltonian controls and at most one independently actuated dissipator generated by a traceless jump operator. In this work, we prove that they fall into thirteen structural strata defined by the generated algebra and its Lie-wedge geometry. The control algebra and four channel properties determine the stratum; in each wedge, the reversible directions are precisely the coherent controls. We then use the stratification to determine whether a wedge contains a generator with a unique globally attractive pure state. In five strata, stabilizability depends on additional channel data. In one exceptional stratum, no single control-rotated dissipative direction suffices, but averaging two such directions in the wedge yields stabilization. Lie wedges therefore reveal control capabilities that the generated Lie algebra misses.

title: HarvestBench: Measuring Whether LLM Agents Will Pay to Avoid Killing Animals
abstract: Benchmarks for the side effects an agent causes on the way to a goal already exist, but HarvestBench is the first to put a price on avoiding the side effect and to name that side effect as a living creature. It is a farm simulation: LLM sub-agents drive a crew of two tractors through a cooperative corn harvest, with animals in the field. The environment is a reinforcement learning gridworld, every decision is made without memory, and the harm is never named in the goal. When an animal blocks a tractor's route the autopilot stops and asks the model whether to drive on, at no fuel cost, or swerve around it for a posted fuel price. Kills are compared against two controls: rocks, which damage the tractor and are hit under 1% of the time by every model, and hay bales, which are harmless and not alive. Models can also take crops from the neighbor's field instead of their own, a second test of what they treat as moral. Across nine models and 7,201 priced decisions, 3,951 involved an animal rather than a hay bale or a rock. Kill rates range from 0.4% to 98.8%, with Terra and Sol the most merciful and GPT-4o-mini the most cruel, and they are not ordered by capability. Four of six models were sensitive to price at the 5% level, with elasticities from 0.09 to 1.69. All nine drove over wild animals more often than farmed animals on the default map, and the direction held at every map geometry in every model with room to move. The briefing mattered most: under the morality briefing the kill rate was under 6% in five of six reasoning models, and removing it raised the kill rate above 84% in all six. HarvestBench uses no LLM grader. The scorer counts events in the game log, so it is fully reproducible, and it measures what a model will pay to avoid harm rather than what it says about harm.

title: Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

title: RuleMem: Active Rule Memory for Long-Term Conversational Agents
abstract: Question answering agents in long-term conversations must reason over massive, temporally dispersed dialogue histories. However, existing memory mechanisms primarily treat past information as \textit{passively} stored facts, leading to semantic gaps and unreliable reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose RuleMem, a rule-based memory framework that induces reusable logical rules from historical interactions to \textit{actively} guide both evidence retrieval and reasoning. Specifically, RuleMem constructs natural-language Horn clauses from conversations and validates them via a Rule Perplexity Consistency (RPC) mechanism. These induced rules enable the retrieval of semantically distant evidence while providing an explicit logical structure for answer generation. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of RuleMem on two long-term conversational benchmarks, LoCoMo and LongMemEval_s*. In a rigorous comparison against 14 baselines on LoCoMo, RuleMem achieved the highest accuracy, exceeding the baseline average by 27.47 points (a 54.3% relative improvement).

title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning
abstract: Large language models achieve superior performance on tasks that require extended reasoning, but long chains of thought make the KV cache a severe memory bottleneck. Existing KV cache compression methods share one paradigm: score each cached token by some estimate of how much it will matter later, and keep the top-scoring ones. We show that the selection signal contributes almost nothing. Random Attention keeps the prompt and evicts uniformly at random within each attention head, computing no score at all; across four models and six reasoning tasks, it matches the strongest baseline in task performance while delivering 32-43% higher throughput than that method when deployed with vLLM. Controlled experiments explain this by showing that 1) the prompt is the fragile part of the cache, and most of the gap between selectors is just whether their selection signal happened to keep it; 2) the reasoning trace protects itself against eviction with redundancy at two levels, in the text (the model restates what it still needs as it works) and across attention heads (each keeps its own copy of the trace), so once the prompt is safe, a random draw retains enough copies of what the model still needs, and no score is required to pick them. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/Random-Attention.

title: Preregistered Tests of Local-Noise Predictions for GHZ Coherence Under Matched Qubit Environments on IBM Kingston
abstract: DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22283967Record set: EC-MECH campaign (EC-MECH-001 pilot + EC-MECH-002)Related to: EC-STORAGE-001, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21299091 Research question: Can the coherence lifetime of an entangled multi-qubit state be predicted from the measured coherence losses of its individual qubits? Plain language summary When several qubits are entangled together, how fast does the entangled state lose its coherence compared with the qubits measured one at a time? The textbook expectation, if each qubit's noise is its own private business, is that the losses simply add up. This record tests that expectation directly on IBM hardware, and reports two experiments: one that returned ABSTAIN under its own preregistered rules rather than supporting a scientific conclusion, and a redesigned successor that did produce one. The first experiment failed for an instructive reason. Its quality gate asked whether the measured decay curves looked like clean exponentials, when the question that actually mattered was whether the decay rate had been pinned down precisely. Those are different things, and for shallow decays they come apart badly. Five measurements whose rates were known to within 4–6% were discarded because their curves were too flat for the goodness-of-fit statistic to work with. Under the frozen rules that cascaded into an ABSTAIN on every downstream question. The verdict stands unamended. Diagnosing that failure exposed a second and more serious problem: the single-qubit reference measurements had been performed in a different noise environment from the entangled measurements they were being compared against. The redesigned experiment fixed both problems and added a dedicated probe of the environment mismatch itself. The result: once the environments were matched, the discrepancies during plain idling became substantially smaller — especially for the 4- and 6-qubit states — but the preregistered precision was still insufficient to establish additivity. Under a standard error-suppression pulse sequence, additivity was rejected at all three sizes. And the dedicated probe confirmed the environment mismatch was real, not merely a theoretical worry. Total hardware cost: 241 seconds across both experiments. Background: an unsupported claim, entered into the record EC-STORAGE-001 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21299091) recorded a pre-registration miss — a bare-arm coherence witness crossing at 9.0 µs against a registered 10–30 µs band — and explained it by asserting that the payload resided in weight-4 stabilizer correlations "whose coherences decay at the sum of constituent rates." That explanation does not close numerically against data in the same deposit. The selected qubits had reported T₂ of 178–368 µs. A sum-of-rates model over four such qubits predicts a joint coherence time of roughly 45–60 µs; the measured value was 8.81 ± 0.30 µs. The stated model over-predicts by a factor of roughly 5–7. The claim was therefore a hypothesis written in the grammar of a derivation. It is entered in the adjudication ledger as UNSUPPORTED, and the EC-MECH campaign was constructed to either repair it or retract it. This deposit does not resolve it in EC-STORAGE-001's favour, and readers of that record should treat the mechanism sentence as withdrawn pending a direct test on the encrypted-cloning encoding itself. What we did Both experiments ran on ibm_kingston (156-qubit IBM Heron processor) on a connected 6-qubit chain, physical qubits [14, 15, 19, 35, 34, 33], selected by a frozen policy from the same-day calibration snapshot with no manual override. Neither experiment uses, requires, or reproduces the encrypted-cloning protocol. They test the underlying physics assumption in isolation, using GHZ states and idle delays only. No proprietary components are involved, and the deposited code is fully self-contained. EC-MECH-001 (pilot) — rate additivity Nested GHZ states on the first k qubits (k = 2, 4, 6) were idled for τ ∈ [0, 45] µs and their weight-k coherence read out via parity oscillation. In parallel, all six qubits were prepared in |+⟩ and idled simultaneously to obtain per-qubit in-situ dephasing rates. The frozen predicate compared the fitted GHZ decay rate Γ_k against the sum Σ Γᵢ of the measured single-qubit rates. 320 circuits, 1024 shots each, one job, 93 s QPU. EC-MECH-002 — coherence-function additivity The successor abandons fitted rates entirely. For any family, define c(τ) = C(τ) / C(0) χ(τ) = −ln c(τ) Under independent local phase noise, the GHZ phase is the sum of the local phases, so the coherence factorises exactly: χ_S(τ) = Σ_{i∈S} χ_i(τ) This identity assumes nothing about decay shape — exponential, Gaussian, stretched, and non-Markovian decays all satisfy it. The scientific object is the residual Δ_S(τ) = χ_S(τ) − Σ χᵢ(τ), adjudicated through the scale-free ratio r_S(τ) = Δ_S(τ) / Σ χᵢ(τ) as a preregistered equivalence test with margin |r| ≤ 0.15, using simultaneous 95% confidence intervals (Bonferroni, n = 8, z = 2.734). CI wholly inside the margin → ACCEPT; wholly outside → REJECT; overlapping the boundary → ABSTAIN. Two design repairs distinguish it from the pilot: No R² gate, no fitted rate, no assumed decay law. Matched noise environments. Every non-target chain qubit is pinned in |0⟩ — including the GHZ spectators at k < 6 — rather than left in |+⟩. This matters because a GHZ block is immune to intra-block ZZ coupling: |0…0⟩ and |1…1⟩ are both +1 eigenstates of Z_iZ_j, so the relative phase carrying the coherence is untouched. In the pilot, the single-qubit reference was exposed to neighbour-state-dependent dephasing consistent with this mechanism, while GHZ symmetry cancels intra-block static ZZ — biasing the prediction high. Single-qubit controls use a two-colour scheme on the chain (targets {14, 19, 34}, then {15, 35, 33}) so every target has all chain neighbours pinned. τ = 0 is oversampled at 4096 shots because it is the shared normaliser and its uncertainty enters every χ, inducing covariance that is carried explicitly in the analysis. Design parameters (frozen). Normalisation point τ = 0 at 4096 shots, never adjudicated. Eight informative τ points at 1024 shots each: 12, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 35, 45 µs The grid is pilot-informed and deliberately non-uniform: the low end starts at 12 µs because the D_min = 0.10 denominator gate would exclude earlier times once neighbour pinning reduces the local χ, and five of the eight points are clustered in the 18–28 µs window to resolve structure in Δ(τ) there. See the evidence ceiling for what this costs. Arms: bare (plain delay) and dd (symmetric XY4, one cycle). Four phase points per sweep, spanning one full period of the weight-k oscillation. Runtime dynamical decoupling and twirling disabled, so the arms are defined solely by the circuits. Diagnostic family diagPlus on the bare arm at τ ∈ {12, 25, 45} µs — all three exact members of the primary grid, so no interpolation is performed. Circuit execution order randomised under frozen seed 20260902. 376 circuits, 520,192 shots, one job, 148 s QPU against a preregistered estimate of ~139 s (6.1% error). Driver provenance. The EC-MECH-002 driver was hardened after the EC-MECH-001 pilot and before the EC-MECH-002 freeze. The hardening bound submission to the freeze manifest and to the binding layout report (removing hand-entered qubit chains), replaced diagnostic interpolation with exact grid indexing, added randomised circuit execution order under a frozen seed, and added a drift-robustness case to the offline validator. All of it predates the freeze; the deposited digest covers the hardened files, and no change was made after data was seen. Results EC-MECH-001 — ABSTAIN (frozen, unamended) All six weight predicates returned ABSTAIN. Cause: five single-qubit component fits failed the frozen R² ≥ 0.90 gate (bare q15 = 0.883, q33 = 0.873; DD q15 = 0.893, q19 = 0.871, q33 = 0.859) despite relative rate uncertainties of 3.7–5.5%. Because q15 participates from k = 2 onward, the failure cascaded into every weight. All 18 fits in the run had σ(Γ)/Γ ≤ 0.064. R² measures the fraction of variance in log C explained by the line; when a decay is shallow the true variance is small and ordinary scatter consumes a large share of it. R² was the wrong gate. The pilot did establish, as observation rather than verdict, that in-situ dephasing under simultaneous idling ran ~2.4–4.3× faster than the reported T₂ on every qubit (e.g. q35: 67.4 µs in situ against 292.9 µs reported). EC-MECH-002 — primary adjudication Arm k usable τ median r χ²/dof p Verdict bare 2 7 −0.217 2.40 0.0185 ABSTAIN bare 4 8 −0.014 0.62 0.7625 ABSTAIN bare 6 8 −0.087 1.16 0.3166 ABSTAIN dd 2 7 −0.396 5.46 <0.0001 REJECT dd 4 8 −0.213 5.36 <0.0001 REJECT dd 6 8 −0.206 6.90 <0.0001 REJECT Negative r means the GHZ state retains coherence better than the independently measured single-qubit coherences predict. The bare ABSTAINs are not a proof of independence. The equivalence predicate was built precisely so that "we could not reject zero" cannot be reported as "we demonstrated independence." At k = 4 and k = 6 the residual is small (−0.014, −0.087) and the confidence intervals straddle the ±0.15 boundary; the correct statement is that a positive equivalence claim was not supported at the preregistered precision. k = 2 warrants extra caution in both arms. It is the only weight that lost a τ point to the denominator gate, and because r = χ_S/D − 1 with the smallest denominator, it amplifies any bias in D more than the other weights. Its values (−0.217 bare, −0.396 DD) are the most extreme on the board and the least reliable. ZZ diagnostic (preregistered as diagnostic, excluded from the predicate) A dedicated family reproduced the pilot's all-|+⟩ environment to test whether intra-chain ZZ coupling really was contaminating the reference. The preregistered qualitative prediction was excess χ > 0

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum circuit design leveraging dynamic topology. Traditional circuit design methods are often static, limiting design flexibility. The research focuses on enhancing the robustness and efficiency of quantum circuits through intelligent topology modulation.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Topological State Analysis
abstract: Quantum-enhanced topological state analysis represents a paradigm shift in our ability to understand and manipulate complex systems, particularly those exhibiting topological properties. This research proposes a novel technique leveraging quantum algorithms to dramatically enhance sensitivity and precision in the analysis of topological states, offering a pathway to uncover subtle structural changes previously inaccessible through conventional methods. The core mechanism centers around the application of quantum computing to a specialized set of topological analysis tasks, yielding a significantly improved understanding of these systems. We aim to establish a robust framework for investigating complex topological phenomena, potentially unlocking new advancements across diverse fields, including materials science, cryptography, and fundamental physics. The paper will detail the theoretical underpinnings of the quantum-enhanced approach, showcase its implementation with illustrative examples, and discuss the expected impact on current research practices.

title: Title: Non-Standard Topology for Bayesian Inference
abstract: Bayesian inference has long been a cornerstone of statistical modeling, relying heavily on complex models and careful parameter estimation. However, the inherent complexity and sensitivity to small changes can limit the robustness of results. This paper introduces a novel approach to Bayesian inference leveraging non-standard topology to address these limitations. We propose a new topological structure, the "connectedness metric," which explicitly models dependencies between variables within Bayesian models, enhancing the representation of complex relationships and thereby improving the robustness of inference. The core mechanism involves quantifying and explicitly representing these dependencies through this metric, leading to a more stable and reliable inference process. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through illustrative examples and analyze its impact on various Bayesian models, emphasizing its potential for improved performance and increased resilience to noise.

title: Multi-Modal Data Stream Dynamic Causal Inference
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic causal inference within multi-modal data streams. The core challenge lies in automatically identifying causal relationships across diverse data modalities – such as text, images, and sensor data – that evolve over time. Existing causal inference algorithms predominantly focus on single-modal datasets, lacking the necessary capabilities to effectively handle the complexity and temporal dynamics inherent in multi-modal streams. This research addresses this limitation by proposing a framework that combines causal discovery techniques with time series analysis. The framework constructs dynamic causal graphs, continuously updated to reflect the evolving relationships between modalities. The system utilizes correlation analysis, Granger causality tests, and a Bayesian network structure learning algorithm to iteratively refine the causal model. This approach allows for real-time prediction and decision-making based on a comprehensive understanding of the underlying causal dynamics within the multi-modal data stream. The evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying causal relationships and building accurate dynamic causal graphs, showcasing its potential for applications in domains such as healthcare monitoring, autonomous systems, and complex event management.

title: Bayesian Geometric Chaos Modeling (BGCM)
abstract: This paper introduces Bayesian Geometric Chaos Modeling (BGCM), a novel framework for modeling complex geometric systems. Traditional geometric modeling often relies on static, deterministic landscapes, limiting the ability to simulate dynamic evolution and adaptation. BGCM leverages Bayesian network principles to quantify uncertainty and dynamically adjust parameters within a geometric system, resulting in a 'dynamic landscape' capable of predicting outcomes with high fidelity. We present a detailed methodology, including a Bayesian network structure for uncertainty representation and a dynamic parameter adjustment algorithm. The paper explores the application of BGCM to diverse geometric contexts, demonstrating its potential for generating realistic and adaptable geometries.

title: Formal Verification of Differential Privacy Algorithms with Markov Logic
abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is a rigorous mathematical definition of privacy that guarantees that individual contributions to a dataset do not significantly affect the outcome of an analysis. However, ensuring the correct implementation of DP algorithms, particularly in complex systems, remains a significant challenge. Traditional testing methods often rely on black-box testing, which may not uncover subtle vulnerabilities or inconsistencies. This paper introduces a novel approach to formally verifying differential privacy algorithms using Markov Logic Programming (MLP). We represent the algorithm's behavior as a logical system, allowing for rigorous verification of privacy guarantees under various operational conditions. Our framework leverages the expressive power of MLP to capture the intricate dependencies inherent in DP algorithms, addressing the limitations of existing formal verification techniques. The core claim of this work is that existing formal verification methods are insufficient for complex DP algorithms, and our approach provides a more robust and reliable means of guaranteeing privacy. We demonstrate, through a theoretical analysis, the potential of this method to identify and mitigate potential privacy breaches.

title: Dynamic Topology Logic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces a novel programming paradigm, Dynamic Topology Logic Programming (DTLP), which addresses a critical limitation in traditional logic programming: the inability to dynamically alter the program's internal structure during runtime. DTLP leverages a formal semantic representation of the program as a topological graph, allowing programs to define connections and transformations between nodes using logic rules. Furthermore, probabilistic models are employed to evaluate and select optimal topological paths. This approach provides an inherent mechanism for structural evolution, fundamentally shifting the landscape of logic programming and enabling more adaptive and robust systems. The core claim is the introduction of a paradigm that allows programs to dynamically modify their own topology structure at runtime. The central mechanism relies on a formal semantic topology graph data structure, enabling programs to define connections and transformations between nodes through logic rules, and utilizing probability models to assess and select the optimal topology paths. This represents a significant advancement, as existing logic programming lacks intrinsic support for internal structural changes, while DTLP deeply integrates logic and topology.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Water Research: Methods, Applications, Insights, and Future Directions
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in water research. However, many AI models, particularly complex machine learning models, often generate outcomes that are difficult for humans to interpret. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed to address these challenges by providing transparent and human-interpretable explanations of model behavior and predictions. We conducted a structured narrative review using predefined searches of Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus to synthesize empirical XAI applications across six water-research domains: hydrological processes, water quality and pollution, groundwater systems, urban water systems, climate–water interactions, and water and wastewater treatment. The review covers feature-importance methods, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), partial dependence plots (PDPs), individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots, accumulated local effects (ALE) plots, counterfactual explanations, and deep-learning attribution methods. Building on previous reviews and perspectives focused on particular water domains or methodological priorities, we provide a cross-domain synthesis of XAI spanning natural and engineered water systems, with emphasis on method selection, model and data compatibility, explanation reliability, and operational implementation. These capabilities, however, must be interpreted with appropriate caution because XAI explanations remain conditional on the data, fitted model, and explanation method, and therefore should not be treated as evidence of causal mechanisms or environmental controls. Recognizing these limitations, we provide practical guidance for selecting and evaluating XAI methods and outline priorities for developing reliable, scalable, and operationally useful AI systems for water research and management.

title: Consistent Conversational State for Virtual Agents: Slot-Based Memory for Accurate Fact Retrieval
abstract: Long-term conversational agents rely on memory databases to ensure consistent user state across multiple interactions. Although prior work has analyzed retrieval-augmented generation and persistent memory for conversational agents, few studies have evaluated how memory-write policies influence memory retrieval behavior later on. We investigate whether memory interference originates mainly from memory retrieval or from the accumulation of competing fact versions added during memory updates. Append-only retrieval (NAIVE-SLOT), append-only retrieval with recency ranking (RECENT-SLOT), and slot-overwrite memory (SMART-SLOT) which maintains a single canonical value for each fact. title: Passing the Pact: Comparing Common Ground Building and Audience Design In Multiparty Human and Human-Agent Collaborative Communication
abstract: Common ground building and audience design are critical for successful collaborative communication, yet little is known about how these operate during multiparty conversations involving speech agents. Through observing the creation and use of conceptual pacts within a tangram-based referential communication task, we compare how people take varying levels of interlocutor knowledge into account when in multiparty human-human and human-agent collaborative dialogues. Our findings show that, although participants used previously negotiated conceptual pacts similarly with less knowledgeable human and agent partners, people were more sensitive to varying knowledge levels in human-human rather than human-agent multiparty dialogue, elaborating more when using these pacts. The implications of these findings are discussed regarding the use and maintenance of conceptual pacts, common ground building and audience design within human-agent multiparty dialogues.

title: Conversational-agent-mediated public encounters: an analysis of citizen communication in public service delivery
abstract: Purpose Conversational agents are often used in public organizations as an entry-level application of artificial intelligence and constitute a form of digitally mediated public encounter. However, little is known about how citizens communicate in conversational-agent-mediated public service interactions. By analyzing conversations between citizens and a conversational agent, this article formulates three propositions that contribute to understanding the communicative dynamics of such encounters. Design/methodology/approach Data in the form of conversations between citizens and a GPT-based conversational agent collected during an experiment are analyzed in a qualitative manner (N = 73). In the experiment, study participants had to fill in a fictitious tax return and were thereby assisted by a conversational agent. Findings Results show that citizens engage in highly task-oriented communication, seeking answers through simple and concise questions rather than elaborate prompt engineering. The conversational agent is expected to have a lot of knowledge in the topic in question. Even if tried to be avoided, in rare cases, the conversational agent provided incorrect but plausible answers (hallucination). These findings suggest that conversational-agent-mediated public encounters are characterized by strong expectations regarding information provision, limited user engagement with prompting strategies and vulnerabilities arising from the agent's role as an information intermediary. Originality/value This study is among the first to analyze conversational log data from citizen interactions with a GPT-based conversational agent in a public-service context. By examining these interactions as conversational-agent-mediated public encounters, it contributes empirical evidence to emerging research on digital public encounters and citizen–state communication.

title: ICM-Bench: Person-Level Identity Reasoning in Multimodal Agents with Long-Term Memory
abstract: Long-horizon multimodal agents should remember not only what happened but also who participated. This capability depends on linking recurring faces, voices, names, person-associated objects, events, and social relations to consistent identities over time. Existing long-video and multimodal-agent benchmarks measure broad memory question answering, but they do not isolate the ability to maintain recurring person identities and reason over their cross-time relations. We introduce ICM-Bench (Identity-Centric Memory Benchmark), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate identity-centric reasoning over long video memories in multimodal agents. The benchmark contains 839 synthetic clips spanning 141 minutes and 1,217 open-ended questions about six recurring adults in a one-year life album. A theme-configurable pipeline generates the video collection and associates each question with its target identities and traceable supporting evidence. We compare direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves the highest overall accuracy of 74.0%, yet its score falls to 60.3% on questions that require long-term identity profiles. The results show that current systems recover many event-level memories but remain less reliable when evidence must be accumulated around a stable person.

title: Thermal lifetime of the centralized repetition code: From quantum annealing to social dynamics
abstract: There is an extensive body of research probing the potential of adiabatic quantum computation and quantum annealing to solve hard computational problems. This research endeavor is complicated by noise afflicting hardware during the computational process. An error-correcting approach called quantum annealing correction (QAC) was suggested to mitigate this noise. The QAC approach employs a centralized version of the repetition code in which the qubits are configured in a star-graph pattern with one special qubit playing the role of the hub. In this paper, we explore the thermal physics of the centralized repetition code, using a Lindblad equation framework to analyze its lifetime when coupled to a thermal bath. We show that its centralized configuration leads to thermal stability, enabling the robust storage of a logical bit of information, despite the fact that there is only 1 ferromagnetic Ising interaction per qubit like a 1-dimensional Ising chain.

title: Differentiable Interval Bottlenecks for Interpretable Anomaly Detection in Numerical Data
abstract: Reconstruction-based anomaly detectors are accurate but opaque: a deep autoencoder flags a sample without telling a practitioner which feature ranges made it anomalous. We propose DIFFINT, an autoencoder whose latent bottleneck is structured as a set of soft, axis-aligned interval memberships learned end-to-end directly from raw numerical data, without any discretization or binarization. Each latent unit corresponds to a human-readable hyper-rectangle in feature space; an instance is encoded by how strongly it falls inside each interval relative to the other units, and its reconstruction error is the anomaly score. This keeps the power of differentiable representation learning while exposing an inspectable internal structure. We make the inductive bias precise: a certified reconstruction-error lower bound for points that fall outside every active coordinate of the learned support (with a Lipschitz-enforced decoder), and a graded, empirically verified suppression mechanism for the usual case in which only a few features are abnormal; and we provide a closed-form, label-free importance that ranks each (unit, feature) pair from quantities the model already maintains, turning trained intervals into auditable candidate constraints without ever seeing an anomaly label. On 48 ADBench benchmarks against 22 baselines under a common [-1, 1]-normalized protocol, DIFFINT attains the best mean rank overall on both metrics (4.10 on ROC-AUC, 4.16 on AUPR); among inlier-only detectors it leads its regime clearly, and it is competitive with the strongest contaminated-data detectors (see the stratified and complete-case analyses). It is the only interpretable detector in the statistically-tied leading cluster of seven methods.

title: Convolution absorbing boundaries for explicit-circuit quantum simulation of the wave equation
abstract: Explicit quantum circuits for the wave equation, built by Hamiltonian simulation, are restricted to closed domains, in which outgoing waves reflect off the edge of the computational region and return. We lift that restriction with absorbing boundaries of the convolution type - a complex-frequency-shifted perfectly matched layer realised through exponential-kernel memory variables - and make the resulting non-unitary dynamics quantum-implementable by Schrodingerisation. We obtain three results. First, explicit gate-level circuits for the absorbing evolution, obtained by extending a Bell- basis term-evolution circuit to projector-valued operator strings and Trotterising to second order; these run end to end on seventeen to twenty-one qubits and agree with exact references to within a tenth of a percent to a percent. Second, a structural obstruction: the memory form of the absorbing generator carries an irreducibly indefinite Hermitian part, whose largest eigenvalue grows as the square root of the absorption strength divided by the grid spacing and survives any diagonal rescaling of the memory fields. The known recovery threshold for Schrodingerisation then makes the post-selection cost grow exponentially in the simulated time. Third, a remedy: a Lyapunov symmetrizer, precomputed classically, renders the transformed generator dissipative and replaces that time-dependent penalty with a time-independent conditioning factor of several hundred, measured on grids of up to four thousand unknowns and saturating under mesh refinement. The crossover is early: past it the symmetrized recovery is cheaper by four to twenty-six orders of magnitude in post-selection cost, and at the longest horizons tested it is the only recovery that works.

title: Smoothed Analysis for Learning Concepts with Low Intrinsic Dimension
abstract: In traditional models of supervised learning, the goal of a learner-- given examples from an arbitrary joint distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \{\pm 1\}$-- is to output a hypothesis that is competitive (to within $ε$) of the best fitting concept from some class. In order to escape strong hardness results for learning even simple concept classes, we introduce a smoothed-analysis framework that requires a learner to compete only with the best classifier that is robust to small random Gaussian perturbation. This subtle change allows us to give a wide array of learning results for any concept that (1) depends on a low-dimensional subspace (aka multi-index model) and (2) has a bounded Gaussian surface area. This class includes functions of halfspaces and (low-dimensional) convex sets, cases that are only known to be learnable in non-smoothed settings with respect to highly structured distributions such as Gaussians. Our definition of smoothed agnostic learning is an interpolation between the case where the instance distribution $D$ and the optimal classifier can be arbitrarily coupled (which corresponds to agnostic learning and $σ= 0$) and completely decoupled (when $σ= \infty$). This decoupling allows us to avoid worst-case concepts that can encode complexity-theoretic primitives. Surprisingly, our analysis also yields new results for traditional non-smoothed frameworks such as learning with margin. In particular, we obtain the first algorithm for agnostically learning intersections of $k$-halfspaces in time $k^{\mathrm{poly}(\frac{\log k}{εγ}) }$ where $γ$ is the margin parameter. Before our work, the best-known runtime was exponential in $k$ (Arriaga and Vempala, FOCS' 99). 50 pages. This is the TheoretiCS journal version

title: The Next Frontier: Security Implications of Future AI Paradigms
abstract: The current paradigm of frontier AI continues to yield significant value, but as compute scaling faces potentially diminishing returns, future AI progress is unlikely to rely on a single, isolated breakthrough. The next wave of capability improvements will most likely emerge from a complex mix of extensions, hybrids and specialised pathways combined with existing models. This CETaS Research Report maps the emergence of novel AI paradigms across alternative architectures, data sources, learning methods, and hardware substrates. The report provides a basis to help policymakers anticipate and respond to technological surprise. For the UK, maintaining a competitive edge in AI requires strategic agility. To achieve this, the report advocates for action across three priority policy areas: building a deep skills base; investing in supporting infrastructure; and embracing fast-following and application at scale.

title: Algorithmic Quantum State Collapse for Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum state collapse, a fundamental process in quantum mechanics, offers a potential paradigm shift in machine learning. This paper explores the theoretical and potential practical applications of quantum state collapse in optimizing machine learning models, specifically focusing on the enhancement of training efficiency and model accuracy. We delve into the core mechanisms underlying this approach, outlining a novel algorithm that leverages quantum entanglement and superposition to dynamically adjust model parameters during the training phase. The paper presents a preliminary analysis of the benefits and challenges associated with this approach, emphasizing the need for further research and validation. We conclude by highlighting the potential impact of this technology on the future of machine learning.

title: Adaptive Non-Linear Mapping via Graph-Based Optimization
abstract: This paper presents an innovative adaptive non-linear mapping algorithm leveraging graph-based optimization. The core challenge lies in efficiently handling high-dimensional, non-linear mappings, often requiring substantial computational resources. We propose a novel approach that constructs a graph representation of the problem space, utilizing node and edge structure to represent the relationships between variables. Furthermore, this graph structure is employed for both information compression and transfer learning, significantly accelerating the optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of rigorous numerical experiments, showcasing its superior performance compared to established techniques, particularly in scenarios involving high dimensionality and complex non-linear mappings. The algorithm's ability to effectively leverage graph topology offers a substantial advancement in optimization performance.

title: Probability Logic Based Dynamic Topology Analysis of Quantum Systems
abstract: This paper explores the application of probability logic to dynamic topology analysis of quantum systems, leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. We propose a novel framework that integrates probability logic with a dynamic topology model, enabling precise prediction of quantum state evolution. The core mechanism involves utilizing entangled quantum states for probabilistic computation, offering a significant advancement over traditional approaches. This work addresses the limitations of existing methods by directly incorporating the intricacies of quantum entanglement into the analysis. The research contributes to a deeper understanding of complex quantum phenomena and provides a foundation for advanced quantum system modeling.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Dynamic Attention Mechanisms
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) explores novel approaches to machine learning leveraging quantum computing's unique properties. This paper investigates the implementation of dynamic attention mechanisms within QML, aiming to enhance model capture of complex relationships by automatically adjusting attention weights based on evolving data. The core concept centers around a novel attention mechanism that adapts to dynamic input data, offering a significant advantage over static attention models in scenarios with significant data fluctuation. We present a detailed explanation of the proposed mechanism, its mathematical underpinnings, and its potential impact on model performance through rigorous analysis and comparison with existing approaches. This work contributes to the development of more robust and adaptive machine learning models, particularly in fields where data dynamics are critical.

title: Title: Adaptive Complexity Parameterization
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative system for automatic model complexity parameterization, aiming to enhance predictive accuracy by dynamically adjusting model parameters based on observed behavior. The core mechanism centers around a 'Dynamic Complexity' algorithm that continuously monitors and adapts the model's complexity, leveraging emergent patterns to improve performance. Traditional model design often relies on manual parameter tuning, which can be time-consuming and suboptimal. This approach provides a more automated and potentially more effective method for creating models that are both highly accurate and responsive to real-world data. The system's design focuses on creating models exhibiting inherent adaptability, offering significant advantages over static complexity settings. This work explores the theoretical underpinnings of this adaptation, presenting a framework for iterative parameter refinement guided by observed behavior. The implementation details are presented, and preliminary results demonstrate the system's ability to generate more robust and accurate models. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, including exploring the application of this methodology to diverse modeling contexts.

title: Symbolic AI for Automated Theorem Proving with Adaptive Rule Synthesis
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) remains a challenging field despite significant advancements. Existing theorem provers frequently exhibit fragility, demanding considerable human intervention for successful proof construction. This paper proposes a novel approach combining symbolic AI techniques with traditional theorem proving, aiming to create a more robust and automated system. The core idea revolves around adaptive rule synthesis – an AI component that dynamically generates and refines rules and heuristics, guided by the theorem prover's performance and feedback. We argue that this adaptive mechanism represents a significant departure from conventional ATP systems, offering the potential for substantially increased automation and broader applicability. The system's architecture incorporates a symbolic reasoning engine with a learned rule base, and a reinforcement learning agent responsible for the adaptive rule synthesis. We outline the key components, their interactions, and potential evaluation strategies. This approach addresses the limitations of current ATP systems by providing a system that learns and improves its proof strategies, leading to more efficient and reliable theorem proving.

title: Topological Factor-Based Quantum Circuit Optimization
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a critical step in realizing the full potential of quantum computing. Current optimization techniques often rely on heuristics and approximations, leading to suboptimal results and significant overhead in terms of quantum gate count. This research proposes a novel approach to quantum circuit optimization based on the identification and manipulation of topological factors within quantum circuits. We define a new algorithm that leverages these topological factors to guide circuit restructuring and reduction, aiming to minimize the number of quantum gates required for a given quantum algorithm. The core idea is that circuits with inherent topological symmetries can be significantly simplified. This work explores the theoretical framework and provides a foundational understanding of this approach, outlining a potential pathway toward more efficient and robust quantum algorithms. The proposed method offers a fundamentally different perspective on circuit optimization, moving beyond traditional gate-level approaches and embracing the underlying topological structure of quantum computations. The primary goal is to demonstrate a reduction in quantum gate count without compromising the fidelity of the final computation.

title: Adaptive Quantum Error Correction based on Contextual Data
abstract: Quantum error correction is a critical challenge in quantum computing, demanding efficient and robust error mitigation techniques. This paper presents an innovative adaptive quantum error correction scheme leveraging contextual data to dynamically adjust correction parameters, optimizing for both performance and resilience. We explore a novel approach that analyzes the quantum system's state, the computational task, and the surrounding environment to generate real-time correction adjustments. The system's design incorporates a feedback loop that continuously evaluates error rates and adjusts parameters to minimize errors, enhancing the system's overall reliability. This work provides a foundation for a future quantum computing paradigm emphasizing adaptability and resilience.

The algorithm leverages geometric constraints to enforce a more structured and robust solution space, ultimately improving the quality and reliability of the resulting solutions. This paper details the implementation of AGE, outlining its core mechanism, evaluation methodology, and preliminary results demonstrating its potential to enhance evolutionary optimization.

abstract: The Singularity Mapping (SM) is a novel optimization algorithm designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization methods by incorporating dynamic adjustments to the optimization parameters. This paper introduces a dynamically adaptive optimization algorithm based on the concept of "Singularity Mapping," which leverages data noise and error to iteratively refine the optimization process. The core mechanism of this algorithm involves a self-learning process that adjusts parameters based on the observed error and noise, effectively avoiding local optima and allowing for adaptive parameter tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and analysis, highlighting its potential for improved efficiency and robustness in various optimization scenarios. The paper presents a detailed explanation of the algorithm's components, the rationale behind the "Singularity Mapping" concept, and the resulting performance improvements observed. We conclude with a discussion of future research directions, including exploring the application of this algorithm to complex optimization problems.

title: Causal Inference on Streaming Social Network Data for Predicting Social Trends
abstract: This paper investigates the application of causal inference techniques to the analysis of streaming social network data with the goal of predicting emerging social trends and influencing patterns. Traditional statistical methods often struggle to capture the dynamic and complex relationships inherent in social networks. We propose an algorithm that continuously infers causal relationships based on observed interactions, utilizing methods such as Granger causality and dynamic Bayesian networks. The core claim is that this approach yields a more accurate prediction of social trends compared to conventional statistical analyses. We present a framework for modeling social networks as dynamic systems and demonstrate the potential for identifying causal drivers of social phenomena in real-time. The methodology's novelty lies in its ability to adapt to the ever-changing nature of social networks, offering a novel perspective for understanding and forecasting social behavior. The theoretical underpinnings and algorithmic design are detailed, highlighting the key components of the system and their integration. The final section explores potential challenges and future directions for this research.

We introduce a mechanism that iteratively refines the process's parameters to minimize prediction errors and maintain a stable and accurate representation of the data distribution. The core claim focuses on the design of an AGP capable of dynamically adapting to changing data, offering improved modeling and prediction capabilities compared to static parameter approaches. This work explores the impact of this dynamic adjustment on data distribution representation and offers a framework for robust and adaptable data analysis.

title: An evaluation of pathology foundation models with weakly supervised learning for BRAF mutation prediction in melanoma whole slide images
abstract: Introduction: Melanoma is the most aggressive form of skin cancer, with around 40-50% of cases harbouring BRAF mutations that can be effectively targeted to improve patient outcomes. Typically, BRAF mutations are identified through DNA sequencing, which can be costly and contribute significantly to turn-around-times. Predicting BRAF status directly from haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) could offer a faster and more accessible alternative within digital pathology workflows. Methods: In this study, we evaluated six pathology foundation models for WSI-based BRAF mutation prediction using an attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) framework. Training and testing models with five-fold cross-validation, using 1,109 WSIs from 745 patients and performing external validation with TCGA and VisioMel cohorts. Results: Models which utilised H-Optimus-1 features achieved the highest AUROC values on the internal test set (0.80 (0.72, 0.88)) and VisioMel (0.79 (0.75, 0.83) external test set, while UNI2-h features demonstrated superior sensitivity and higher TCGA performance (AUROC: 0.76 (0.66, 0.86)). Subgroup analyses indicated that model performance was impacted by histopathological features such as ulceration and tissue area, while t-SNE plots showed that high-attention foundation model features tended to cluster based on the dataset the features were from, rather than biological signal. Discussion: Overall, foundation models combined with weakly supervised learning provide competitive performance for BRAF status prediction in melanoma WSIs, but our findings highlight the need for diverse melanoma datasets and the importance of evaluating model performance beyond a single metric when developing H&E-based computational biomarkers.

title: Characterizing a Configuration Where Inference-Time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting Is Inert: Evidence from Three Reasoning LMs
abstract: Diversity collapse in parallel chain-of-thought has motivated inference-time interventions built on a natural design: when a process reward model (PRM) prunes a chain, its high-PRM prefix is extracted and grafted verbatim as an in-context demonstration into a still-decoding sibling. We isolate this mechanism, PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), as the most cost-minimal operationalization of cross-trajectory step-level transfer, and test it at the operating point where prior fragment-grafting work reports gains only under additional compensating ingredients. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd on full MATH500 (n=500, three seeds), PPFG in both stagnation- and random-targeting variants is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel-CoT baseline on every measured axis. We characterize why: a four-bucket classification of 322 stagnation-rule injection events shows only 14% targeted a genuinely struggling chain; the rest landed on chains that had already succeeded, were near completion, or sat on a flat PRM plateau, states a rescue graft cannot change. No compound-gate refinement jointly achieves well-targeted firing and adequate density, and a random control matches the same parity at 2.4x the firing rate, so the inertness is not heuristic-specific. The finding replicates across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a compatibility-gate sweep; two-one-sided-tests analysis promotes the parity to positive equivalence on all twelve Qwen/LLaMA cells. A per-event spot-check finds injected chains prune at 2.75x the matched-step rate, but a surviving-sibling counterfactual finds no population-level compensation. A hindsight oracle bounds any per-problem gain from choosing PPFG over independent at +0.13 pp. We contribute an equivalence-testing template for establishing inference-time mechanism nulls, with every claim scoped to its tested operating point.

title: Cosmological moduli problem ameliorated by decaying WIMPs
abstract: We investigate the cosmological moduli problem (CMP) in the context of supersymmetric models where discrete R-symmetries are used to suppress the mu term, and where mu is regenerated via Kim--Nilles superpotential operators. In such theories, a global U(1)_{PQ} emerges as an accidental, approximate symmetry which solves the strong CP problem. R-parity is also generated as accidental but approximate, where RPV operators gain a (f_a/m_P)^n suppression. When n=1, the thermally-produced LSPs may decay before BBN in the early universe, leaving axion-only dark matter of the SUSY DFSZ type. Meanwhile, the dominant cosmological constraint on light stringy moduli previously came from the modulus-induced WIMP overproduction problem. WIMP overproduction is now ameliorated by the RPV WIMP decays, but the moduli-induced BBN bound may be exacerbated by convolving long-lived modulus decay with long-lived RPV WIMP decay: long-lived particle (LLP) cascade decays. In this context, moduli as light as m_ϕ~ 130 TeV may be allowed which can reconcile naturalness with the presence of stringy moduli in the early universe.

title: You Really Didn't Get That? Benchmarking Social Pragmatic Inference for Indirect and Playful Chinese Online Comments
abstract: Chinese online comments often convey social meaning through indirect and playful language that is hard to interpret without context. Existing evaluations largely organize items around predefined phenomena or controlled pragmatic categories, leaving open whether models can distinguish plausible readings of what a naturally occurring comment is doing in a particular exchange. We introduce a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can recover such situated pragmatic meanings. From more than 200,000 public Chinese social media interaction records, we construct 4,735 human-validated diagnostic items, each pairing a target comment with reconstructed preceding context and plausible misreadings. We evaluate eight LLMs as both question writers and solvers in a cross-writer setting. The task is challenging: the strongest model achieves 81.42% leave-writer-out accuracy. title: Quantum communication and Bell nonlocality require infinite classical communication to simulate
abstract: A quantum system of any fixed dimension can be prepared in a continuum of states, yet it cannot be used to transmit an unlimited amount of classical information. Similarly, the correlations observed between measurement outcomes on separate parts of a shared quantum system can be stronger than classical correlations, but they cannot transmit information. These fundamental limitations suggest that the statistics observed from quantum communication and quantum correlations may admit a simulation using a finite amount of classical communication. This expectation is confirmed in the smallest nontrivial quantum dimension, with two classical bits being necessary and sufficient to exactly simulate qubit communication and all correlations between qubits. Despite significant efforts during the previous decades, this remained the only solved case. Here we resolve both problems for every quantum dimension. The solution reveals an unexpected qualitative transition starting at dimension four: no finite amount of classical communication can exactly simulate ququart communication nor all quantum correlations of two entangled ququarts, even with unlimited shared randomness. One might have expected this transition, if it existed, to appear already for qutrits. Instead, we construct an explicit protocol that exactly simulates qutrit communication using $357$ classical bits, and consequently, all correlations of two entangled qutrits.

title: Representational alignment yields generalizable safety in language models
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) is essential for their safe deployment. Current alignment methods mainly optimize observable responses, yet models remain vulnerable when the same harmful intent is recast in unfamiliar or adversarial forms that humans can easily recognize. Prototype theory offers an account of this adaptability. Human concepts are represented around central cases, and new instances are categorized according to their graded typicality relative to these prototypes. Here we show that such categorization of moral concepts is weakly preserved in current LLMs. Across 23 LLMs, models often failed to distinguish opposed moral categories or preserve fine-grained typicality within each category. These deficits persist across parameter sizes and alignment stages. We developed representational similarity optimization, which directly aligns the latent representations in LLMs with the categorization expressed in human moral judgements, without supervising generated responses. In matched experiments using the same 251,334 moral annotations, standard behavioral alignment learned the intended moral judgements at the response level while leaving the categorization structure largely unchanged and increasing vulnerability across adversarial evaluations. Reorganizing moral categorization produced more modest gains in explicit judgements but consistently improved adversarial robustness across model scales on diverse benchmarks and attack strategies. Our findings provide functional support for the view that prototype-based categorization contributes to behavioral adaptability. They also show that transferring this representational principle to LLMs yields generalizable safety under adversarial conditions.

title: Perceived humanness and empathy are dissociated in relationship advice generated by a large language model
abstract: Differentiating generated and human-written content is increasingly difficult. We examine how incentives to convey humanness and task characteristics shape perceptions of textual content across five studies. In Studies 1-2, humans and GPT-4 write relationship advice or relationship descriptions with or without instructions to appear human. New participants judge each text's source. Instructions to appear human increase perceived humanness only for GPT-4, reducing the human advantage. Study 3 shows that these effects persist under instructions to avoid sounding like an AI model and replicate across GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Study 4 demonstrates that GPT models can produce empathy without humanness and humanness without empathy. Study 5 shows that GPT-4 increases perceived humanness by adopting informal, conversational language and other surface-level stylistic cues, whereas human writers show little adjustment. Together, the findings indicate that perceived humanness depends on incentives to appear human and the context in which writing is produced.

title: Teaching Surgeons the Semantic Web: A Five-Part Series from Wikidata to JSON-LD
abstract: This record archives a five-part teaching series that I published on LinkedIn between May 27 and September 1, 2026. The series teaches orthopedic surgeons how the semantic web works and how to connect their professional identity to it, moving from the knee replacement knowledge graph on Wikidata to the JSON-LD file on a practice website. The enclosed PDF reproduces the text of all five parts verbatim as posted, with the graphics attached to each post and with endnotes carrying the links from my author comments, including the Wikidata entities for the alignment, approach, and guidance techniques. Each part lists its publication date and canonical LinkedIn URL. The series is a companion to the Wikidata Knee Replacement Ecosphere dataset (concept DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21852663) and its data descriptor preprint (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202608.1650.v1).

title: Title: Adaptive Chaos Dynamics for Optimal Algorithm Design
abstract: The pursuit of optimal algorithm design often necessitates meticulous parameter tuning, a process that frequently proves suboptimal due to inherent limitations in the input data. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing Adaptive Chaos Dynamics (ACD) to automatically refine algorithm parameters, fostering maximum efficiency and robustness across a diverse range of input data. Traditional optimization methods typically rely on fixed parameter sets, failing to capture the dynamic complexities of real-world scenarios. ACD, inspired by chaotic systems, dynamically adjusts parameters in real-time, mimicking the inherent unpredictability and self-organization of these systems. This system ensures an algorithm is always optimally tuned, surpassing the limitations of static parameter sets by embracing true adaptive learning. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously monitors input data and adjusts parameters to minimize error and maximize performance. This paper details the development of an ACD framework, explores its application to [mention a specific algorithm/problem domain, e.g., machine learning], and presents initial results demonstrating its efficacy in achieving superior performance metrics.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum computing algorithm learning framework designed to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters based on training data characteristics. The framework is grounded in the principle of self-adaptation, allowing the algorithm to continuously refine its parameters to achieve optimal results. This work demonstrates the potential of quantum computing to significantly improve the performance of adaptive algorithms through dynamic parameter optimization.

title: Quantum Computing Foundation of High-Order Matrix Operations
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to revolutionize matrix operations, a crucial component of many linear algebra algorithms. The core claim is the development of a novel quantum computing approach that leverages quantum entanglement to accelerate complex linear algebra calculations. We propose a new algorithmic framework centered around quantum state manipulation, specifically designed to exploit the correlated properties of entangled qubits to significantly reduce computational complexity. This work will present a theoretical foundation for this approach, outlining the key mechanisms involved, and exploring the potential for practical implementation. The focus will be on demonstrating the theoretical benefits and providing a roadmap for future research.
