title: AdaptVPR: Route-Aware Hard Positive Generation for Robust Visual Place Recognition
abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) localizes a query image by retrieving database images of the same or nearby place, yet its robustness is often degraded by domain shifts arising from illumination, weather, seasonal changes, and dynamic occlusions. One contributing factor is the limited appearance diversity of the same place in existing training data. To address this issue, we propose AdaptVPR, a route-aware generative augmentation framework that constructs same-place hard positives for robust VPR training. AdaptVPR first uses a vision language model to parse scene attributes and estimate editing feasibility, while a rule-based scheduler determines the generation route according to editability scores and risk constraints. The generation process is decomposed into three complementary routes: the Global Appearance Route introduces global scene changes in weather, illumination, and time of day; the Local Occlusion Route inserts plausible dynamic occluders; and the Dual Route combines both types of perturbations to produce more challenging appearance shifts. Each generated candidate is evaluated using a VPR-oriented verification scheme based on geometric consistency and appearance diversity, reducing the risk of structural drift while ensuring sufficient appearance variation. Global candidates are generated once and rejected if verification fails, while Local Occlusion and Dual candidates use verification feedback for limited prompt refinement and regeneration. Using this framework, we construct AdaptCities, containing 160K verified synthetic same-place hard positives. Experiments across multiple VPR baselines and vision foundation backbones show consistent gains on standard benchmarks and substantial improvements under challenging domain shifts, with R@1 gains of up to 9.2%. The source code and data resources are publicly available at https://github.com/chenshunpeng/AdaptVPR.

title: Summary of the ChinaVoices Challenge 2026: Data, Tasks, Baseline, and Methods
abstract: This paper summarizes the ChinaVoices Challenge 2026, which aims to establish unified task definitions and evaluation conditions for Chinese dialect speech processing and to advance multi-dialect identification and automatic speech recognition. The challenge covers 16 dialect categories and defines two tasks: Chinese Multi-Dialect Identification and Chinese Multi-Dialect Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). It uses approximately 320 hours of speech across the Reference Set, Open Evaluation Set, and Hidden Evaluation Set. The two tasks use the same evaluation audio, and each includes restricted-data and open-data tracks. We describe the task settings, data, evaluation metrics, and Qwen3-ASR-1.7B baseline, and analyze the leaderboard results and submitted systems. In total, 28 teams submit results, 17 provide system reports, and systems from 15 teams pass the compliance review and are included in the analysis. Most eligible systems outperform the baseline, and the official top-three order remains unchanged on the Hidden Evaluation Set for both tasks. Dialect-level results show that categories with higher identification accuracy generally have lower ASR error rates, although the tasks assess related but distinct capabilities. Leading identification systems commonly exploit dialect-discriminative acoustic representations, whereas leading ASR systems emphasize data normalization, augmentation, and auxiliary CTC objectives. These results provide practical guidance for developing and evaluating Chinese multi-dialect speech processing systems.

title: The Civilization Framework: Sovereign-Anchored Communication Between Personal Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Humans are the transport layer between AI systems, losing context at every hop. We present the Civilization Framework, whose addressable party is the civilization, not the agent (one human sovereign, a persistent ledger, and interchangeable agents), and the Embassy Protocol, a carrier-agnostic overlay: messages arrive asynchronously at a resident ledger endpoint, any online agent of the receiver handles them, and commitment state on both ledgers, not delivery, is ground truth. Authority derives from memory: an agent's power to act for its civilization is capped by the memory it can access and externalized through signed credentials, separate from civilization-level reputation. We identify the temporal-weight effect, a hazard in AI-to-AI communication where what arrives first acquires unearned authority, and test it in one frontier model in a preregistered 1,908-trial experiment. With verification removed, an incorrect upstream claim arriving first captures 54.2% of answers (4.2% under full verification), while the same claim arriving after the receiver has sealed its own answer captures 31.6% (the two prompt shells are not length-matched, so part of that gap may reflect shell form; see Section 7), and both registered question-set specifications agree on these two verdicts (the exclusion specification is preregistered as under-powered). Two secondary results, the mitigation from instruction-level provenance labeling and sealed-answer accuracy equivalence, are specification-dependent, holding only under the all-questions specification. Because a registered check of tool use failed its call-budget condition, the registration classifies the round as inconclusive and every result above, primary and secondary, is reported as exploratory; a replication with harness-enforced budgets is planned. The framework's intra-civilization layer has a working implementation.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
abstract: When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

title: A Personalized, Adaptive Learning Platform for Tertiary Education
abstract: The continuous increase of digital education has exposed the limitations of traditional, uniform learning models that fail to account for individual learner differences. A Personalised Learning Platform with Adaptive Content (PLPAC), which is AI-driven, was developed to deliver tailored learning experiences through real-time adaptation. The system incorporates the mathematical Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) model, a hybrid collaborative and content-based recommendation engine, and mastery-based progression, adjusting content difficulty, format, sequence, and assessment in response to each learner's evolving profile. The system was built using a five-layer, multi-tier architecture across six two-week Agile sprints, and was then evaluated using a 12-week, mixed-methods, quasi-experimental design involving 250 tertiary-level students (125 in the PLPAC experimental group, 125 in a conventional Learning Management System control group). Results showed statistically significant gains across all four evaluated dimensions: large normalized learning gains for PLPAC (Hake's g = 0.43) relative to the control group (g = 0.20), with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.76); a 42% higher module completion rate (χ²(1) = 38.47, p < .001); substantially higher engagement across six behavioural metrics (77%–225% increases); and a disproportionately larger gain for the lowest-performing quartile of learners, which narrowed the gap in learning gains (though not the absolute post-test score gap) between low- and high-achieving learners relative to the control group. User satisfaction averaged 4.27 out of 5, exceeding the System Usability Scale benchmark.

title: Dynamic Topology-Based Adaptive Learning Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology-based adaptive learning framework designed to enhance learning and modeling capabilities. Traditional learning frameworks often remain static, failing to adapt effectively to evolving data and environments. Our framework leverages dynamic topology, allowing the model to dynamically adjust its structure in response to new information, thereby promoting more efficient learning and representation. This approach overcomes the limitations of static models by providing a mechanism for continuous refinement and adaptation. The core of the framework lies in the implementation of a topology that evolves in response to the input data, ensuring a more robust and adaptable learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing its ability to handle complex data and achieve superior performance compared to existing approaches.

title: 基于动态概率场的混沌几何优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on dynamic probability fields, designed to address challenges in complex, adaptive parameter environments. Conventional optimization methods often struggle with intricate, non-linear problems, necessitating static approaches. We propose a framework where the probability field dynamically adjusts parameters during the optimization process, fostering a more adaptable and responsive optimization trajectory. This algorithm leverages the inherent nonlinearity of the probability field to generate unique paths that can effectively navigate and optimize complex systems. The core mechanism involves utilizing a probabilistic model to guide the optimization process, ensuring a more flexible and robust solution compared to traditional methods. This paper provides a detailed examination of the algorithm's design, implementation, and performance evaluation, showcasing its potential for tackling challenging optimization problems across diverse domains.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Modeling and Extraction
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for information transfer and processing. This paper explores a novel approach to leveraging entanglement for information modeling and extraction, proposing a quantum computation framework based on adaptive computation and a highly efficient information extraction algorithm. We detail the core concept of utilizing entanglement as a communication channel, designing a specialized quantum computation framework, and developing an extraction method that exploits entanglement's properties. The paper introduces a comprehensive mathematical framework and illustrates the algorithm's performance through simulations and preliminary experiments. This work aims to advance the field of quantum information theory by demonstrating the potential of entanglement-based computation and information extraction.

title: Geometric Information Theory: A Quantum Computing Paradigm
abstract: Geometric Information Theory (GIT) offers a novel approach to quantum computation by leveraging geometric structure as a fundamental basis for quantum information. This paper explores the integration of GIT with quantum computing, focusing on the design of a quantum algorithm specifically tailored for efficient processing of large geometric datasets. We present a detailed conceptual framework, outlining the core mechanisms and potential benefits of this hybrid approach. The research demonstrates the feasibility of utilizing geometric structures as a key component of a quantum computation, aiming to significantly enhance computational performance for complex geometric tasks.

title: Wavefunction Collapse Optimization (WCO)
abstract: Wavefunction Collapse Optimization (WCO) is a novel optimization algorithm designed to accelerate the discovery of optimal solutions within complex systems by leveraging the principles of wavefunction collapse. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and time-consuming nature of finding the absolute best solution in these systems. WCO proposes a probabilistic approach, iteratively refining parameters to reduce uncertainty and converge towards optimal configurations, offering a significantly faster and more efficient method for complex problem-solving. This paper details the theoretical framework, implementation details, and preliminary results demonstrating the efficacy of WCO in a variety of scenarios.

title: Quantum Information Storage: Topology Optimization
abstract: Quantum information storage is a challenging and crucial area of research, demanding innovative approaches to overcome limitations in current technologies. This paper explores a novel method for optimizing quantum information storage based on the inherent properties of topological structures. We propose a technique that leverages the unique characteristics of topological phases to enhance storage capacity and data transmission efficiency. The core mechanism centers on manipulating the topology of the quantum state to optimize its resilience and information density. This approach offers a fundamentally different perspective on quantum data storage, potentially unlocking new levels of performance. The paper details the theoretical framework, the implementation of the optimization algorithm, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this method.

title: Dynamic Circuit Synthesis for Quantum Computing based on Graph Representation
abstract: Quantum circuit synthesis is a critical step in quantum computing, aiming to translate a logical quantum circuit into an efficient physical implementation. Traditional methods often suffer from inefficiency and a lack of adaptability, particularly when dealing with varying input data. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum circuit synthesis that leverages graph representation and dynamic adaptation. The core idea is to represent quantum circuits as graphs, allowing the system to analyze and modify the circuit structure in real-time based on the input data. This dynamic adaptation minimizes gate count and execution time, offering significant improvements over static synthesis techniques. The presented framework provides a foundation for more flexible and efficient quantum computation.

abstract: This paper investigates the potential of leveraging chaotic geometry and neural networks to achieve enhanced model generalization and adaptability. We propose a novel architecture that integrates the training process with a dynamic, chaotic evolution of the network's geometry. This approach, termed "混沌拓扑驱动的自适应几何", aims to mitigate the limitations of static parameter tuning and foster neural networks capable of robust responses to changing environments. The paper details the core mechanism – the dynamic geometry adjustment – and explores its potential benefits through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation. We demonstrate that this methodology can significantly improve model performance across a range of tasks, offering a promising pathway toward more intelligent and versatile neural network designs.

title: The Application of Non-Linear Geometric Transformations in Reinforcement Learning for Enhanced Learning Efficiency
abstract: This paper investigates the application of non-linear geometric transformations within reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance learning efficiency and model performance. Traditional RL algorithms often employ static approaches, limiting their adaptability to complex environments. We propose a novel framework that dynamically adjusts the environment state through geometric transformations, enabling the algorithm to optimize its trajectory and achieve superior results. This research explores the potential of incorporating geometric constraints into RL training, offering a pathway towards more robust and efficient learning. The core mechanism focuses on using non-linear transformations to guide the agent's exploration and reward shaping, ultimately improving the learning process. This work represents a significant advancement in RL, introducing a dynamic and spatially aware approach that can overcome limitations of conventional methods.

title: Adaptive Control of Swarm Robotics using Quantum-Inspired Particle Swarm Optimization
abstract: Swarm robotics offers a promising approach to solving complex tasks through collective behavior of simple robots. However, controlling these swarms effectively remains a significant challenge, particularly in dynamic and uncertain environments. Traditional control methods often struggle to adapt to changing conditions or handle the inherent complexities of swarm dynamics. This paper proposes a novel adaptive control strategy for swarm robotics based on a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm enhanced with quantum-inspired concepts. The core idea is to introduce principles of quantum superposition and tunneling into the PSO framework, allowing particles to simultaneously explore multiple potential solution spaces and more effectively escape local minima. This approach aims to improve the robustness, adaptability, and overall performance of the swarm control system. We present the mathematical formulation of the quantum-inspired PSO algorithm, detailing the key modifications and their impact on the optimization process. The proposed method demonstrates enhanced convergence speed and improved ability to handle complex swarm behaviors compared to standard PSO.

title: Dynamically Adaptive Kernel Methods for Non-Stationary Data
abstract: Kernel methods have demonstrated remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. However, their performance often degrades significantly when the underlying data distribution changes over time – a scenario frequently encountered in real-world applications like finance, sensor networks, and time series analysis. This paper addresses this limitation by proposing a dynamically adaptive kernel method. The core idea is to continuously learn and adjust the kernel function used by the method, enabling it to maintain optimal performance even amidst non-stationary data. We introduce a kernel alignment approach, where the kernel function is updated online based on the observed data distribution. The algorithm aims to minimize the divergence between the learned kernel and a reference kernel, effectively adapting to shifts in the data. We formally define the adaptive kernel learning framework, outline the key components of the algorithm, and discuss its theoretical properties. The evaluation of the algorithm relies on simulated and real-world non-stationary datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in preserving the performance of kernel methods when faced with evolving data distributions.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming with Reinforcement Learning for Task Decomposition
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to automated programming, specifically designed for complex tasks that necessitate both symbolic reasoning and numerical computation. The core challenge in automated programming lies in effectively handling intricate task decomposition – a process traditionally reliant on human expertise. We propose a neuro-symbolic system that leverages reinforcement learning to automatically decompose complex tasks. The system incorporates a neural network to learn the decomposition strategy and dynamically generates and refines symbolic rules based on the network's decisions. This approach offers a pathway to automating sophisticated programming challenges, moving beyond the limitations of purely rule-based or data-driven methods. The system's architecture is described, and the core concept of dynamically generating symbolic rules based on neural network outputs is detailed. This work aims to bridge the gap between neural network learning and symbolic programming, leading to more robust and adaptable automated programming systems.

title: Cognitive Graph-Based Automated Causal Reasoning Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to automated causal reasoning within cognitive graphs, leveraging deep learning techniques. The core idea is to construct a cognitive graph and, using deep learning, automatically learn and reason about causal relationships, ultimately enabling prediction and decision-making. We utilize causal graphs as a representation, combined with graph neural networks (GNNs), to facilitate the automatic learning of causal relationships from the graph structure. This approach addresses a significant gap in traditional knowledge graph learning, which predominantly focuses on relational understanding without explicitly capturing causality. The proposed framework offers a pathway to more robust and interpretable AI systems capable of handling complex real-world scenarios where causal understanding is paramount. The primary contribution lies in the integration of causal reasoning into the cognitive graph learning paradigm, offering an automated solution for deciphering causal connections within large, interconnected datasets. The model learns through the propagation of information across the graph, guided by the underlying causal structure. This results in improved predictive accuracy and the ability to generate more informed decisions.

title: Quantum Bioinformatics: Gene Sequence Alignment Based on Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to gene sequence alignment leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement. Traditional gene sequence alignment methods face significant computational challenges, particularly with increasing genome sizes, leading to slow processing times and limitations in accuracy. Our proposed methodology encodes gene sequences into qubits and utilizes quantum entanglement to establish correlations between sequences, dramatically accelerating the alignment process. We present a theoretical framework outlining the core claim, mechanism, and potential advantages of this approach. The theoretical model focuses on exploiting quantum superposition and entanglement to explore the vast solution space of possible alignments concurrently, offering a significant speedup compared to classical algorithms. We detail the mathematical formulation of the entanglement-based alignment process, including the key equations governing the correlation probability and the estimated reduction in computational complexity. The core aim is to demonstrate the feasibility of using quantum entanglement to enhance gene sequence alignment, potentially revolutionizing bioinformatics research and accelerating the discovery of biological insights.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum entanglement network optimization algorithm designed to automatically adjust the topology of quantum entanglement networks to maximize entanglement efficiency and communication capabilities. The core mechanism involves monitoring and dynamically adjusting the network topology based on a set of defined metrics, leading to enhanced entanglement quality and improved communication performance. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and preliminary experimental results, highlighting its potential to significantly improve the performance of quantum communication systems.

title: Causal Bayesian Networks with Latent Variable Propagation for Intervention Analysis
abstract: Traditional Bayesian Networks (BNs) struggle to effectively model and reason about interventions due to their inherent limitations in representing confounding factors and accurately simulating the propagation of causal effects. This paper introduces a novel approach – Causal Bayesian Networks with Latent Variable Propagation – designed to address these shortcomings. The core idea involves extending BNs by incorporating latent variables that represent unobserved confounders. A new algorithm, "Latent Variable Propagation," is then employed to simulate the impact of interventions on the network's causal structure. This framework provides a more realistic and accurate representation for intervention analysis, enabling the assessment of causal effects within complex systems. The method's key contributions are the formalization of a latent variable propagation process and its application within a BN structure, offering a robust tool for causal inference. The presented work lays the groundwork for improved understanding and decision-making in scenarios where interventions are central to the analysis. ---

title: Neural Network Quantum Entanglement Computation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to computation by leveraging quantum entanglement within a simulated neural network. The core idea is to utilize the inherent parallelism of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement, to achieve computational speeds beyond those attainable by classical neural networks. We introduce a model where artificial neurons are interconnected to mimic quantum entanglement, employing quantum algorithms such as Grover's algorithm for distributed computation. The model incorporates neural network synaptic connections to simulate quantum state superposition and interference. The potential for significant computational advantages through this hybrid approach is explored. The key equations demonstrating the core model are presented below: Let $s_i$ represent the state of neuron $i$, where $i = 1, 2, ..., K$. $s_i \in \{0, 1\}$ The entanglement between neurons $i$ and $j$ is represented as: $E_{ij} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \cos(\theta_{ij})$ where $\theta_{ij}$ is the angle of entanglement between neurons $i$ and $j$. The update rule for neuron $i$ is given by: $s_i^{(t+1)} = \sum_{j=1}^{K} G_{ij} s_j^{(t)}$ where $G_{ij}$ is the interaction coefficient between neurons $i$ and $j$. Grover's Algorithm can be represented as: $O = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i \frac{|i\rangle}{\sqrt{|i\rangle\langle i|}}$ where $N$ is the number of qubits. The oracle operator $O$ flips the amplitude of the marked state. The Grover iteration is: $U = \mathcal{I} + 2O + \lambda \sigma_x$ where $\mathcal{I}$ is the identity operator, $\sigma_x$ is the Pauli-X operator, and $\lambda$ is the Grover iteration number.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic space algorithm designed to optimize computationally intensive tasks through adaptive complexity control. Traditional complexity management methods often lack the ability to dynamically adjust to data distribution, necessitating manual tuning. This work proposes a new approach – the "Complexity Module" – that automatically adjusts algorithm parameters based on input data complexity, offering enhanced efficiency and potentially improved performance. We present a framework for defining and implementing this module, demonstrating its effectiveness through a series of simulations and analyses. The core claim is that this algorithm significantly outperforms traditional approaches in scenarios with varying data complexities. This is achieved through a dynamic adjustment of computation steps, data storage, and overall computational burden. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results, emphasizing the benefits of adaptive complexity control.

abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers unprecedented computational capabilities. We demonstrate the algorithm's potential to surpass classical computational limitations by exploiting the inherent dynamism of quantum systems. This work presents a framework for dynamically shaping quantum states, offering a pathway to significantly accelerate computations and enable new quantum algorithms.

abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Topology for Neural Network Representation (ATNR) method designed to dynamically adjust the topology of neural network representations during training. Traditional approaches often treat topology as fixed, limiting the model's ability to adapt to the data. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging a neural network to learn a 'map' of the network's internal structure, which is continuously updated as the training proceeds. We present a framework for training ATNR, detailing the neural network architecture, training procedure, and evaluation results demonstrating its effectiveness. The study explores the impact of different network architectures and training strategies on the performance of ATNR.

title: GRACE: Graph-Grounded Reflective Agent Copilot Engine for Expert-in-the-Loop Knowledge Expansion
abstract: Large language models deployed in high-stakes settings frequently generate plausible but ungrounded claims. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines offer limited remedy, since they retrieve isolated passages without tracking cross-document evidence relationships or quantifying uncertainty. We introduce GRACE (Graph-grounded Reflective Agent Copilot Engine), a framework that deconstructs LLM responses into atomic claims and grounds them against trusted knowledge priors within a weighted bipartite graph. Edge weights encode the closeness of each claim to the priors, enabling weighted centrality analysis that classifies claims as Grounded, Refuted, or Boundary. Such classification identifies not just hallucinations but also novel or contested claims at the frontier of the model's knowledge. To efficiently allocate human or agent resources, we formulate a Return on Attention (RoA) objective that defers a claim to expert review only when its priority-weighted uncertainty exceeds the cost of verification. Claims verified by experts are promoted to new evidence anchors, closing a validator-LLM evolutionary loop that expands the knowledge base across iterations. We evaluate GRACE across multiple language models and on datasets spanning both general and domain-specific knowledge. Our results show that our knowledge base serves as a reliable foundation for retrieval that outperforms RAG baselines, and that the RoA framework efficiently selects valuable boundary knowledge for expert verification. These findings demonstrate that graph-structured representations combined with expert-in-the-loop verification can mitigate hallucination at the system level rather than at the generation level. Code available at https://github.com/johnsk95/grace_code

Claims verified by experts are promoted to new evidence anchors, closing a validator-LLM evolutionary loop that expands the knowledge base across iterations. We evaluate GRACE across multiple language models and on datasets spanning both general and domain-specific knowledge. Our results show that our knowledge base serves as a reliable foundation for retrieval that outperforms RAG baselines, and that the RoA framework efficiently selects valuable boundary knowledge for expert verification. These findings demonstrate that graph-structured representations combined with expert-in-the-loop verification can mitigate hallucination at the system level rather than at the generation level. title: Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier
abstract: We present Iris-mini and Iris-pro, two search agents trained at the 35B-A3B and 397B-A17B scales, together with the data pipeline and training recipe behind them. Tasks are reverse-constructed from the hyperlink structure of a web corpus: we author multi-hop chains over an entity graph distilled from a seed page and its out-links, rewrite every non-answer entity into a descriptive reference so that no clue can be resolved by string matching, and admit only questions that a reference model fails closed-book yet solves once the supporting evidence is supplied. These questions are then turned into trajectories, which are filtered at both the trajectory and the turn level before SFT. The policy is then optimized by RL against live search, with the reward judge and the observation summarizer served inside the training cluster, and with over-long rollouts interrupted at the request level and resumed from their committed prefix at the next step. We alternate the two stages in a procedure we call SFT-RL climbing, returning the hardest solved and most efficient rollouts of each RL round to the next supervised pass. Because inference-time context management is worth more on these benchmarks than most reported differences between systems, we evaluate every benchmark both with and without it, holding the tool set, the context limit, and the judge fixed. All results come from a single ReAct agent, with no sub-agents and no test-time verification. With management enabled, on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE the two models reach 82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3 and 88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4, the strongest overall results among open-source search agents in their respective parameter ranges. We plan to release the model weights together with the complete recipe for data construction, training, and evaluation.

title: String problems in the congested clique model
abstract: In this paper we present algorithms for several string problems in the Congested Clique model. In the Congested Clique model, n nodes (computers) are used to solve some problem. The input to the problem is distributed among the nodes, and the communication between the nodes is conducted in rounds. In each round, every node is allowed to send an $$O(\log n)$$ -bit message to every other node in the network. We consider three fundamental string problems in the Congested Clique model. First, we present an O(1)-round algorithm for string sorting. Second, we present an O(1)-round combinatorial pattern matching algorithm. Finally, we present an $$O(\log \log n)$$ -round algorithm for the computation of the Suffix Array and the corresponding Longest Common Prefix array of a given string. To obtain these algorithms, we develop a sorting procedure for large keys of polynomial size, extending the prior sorting algorithm of Lenzen [PODC’13], which handles only $$O(\log n)$$ -bit keys. This new procedure may be of independent interest.

title: Quantum-Based Geometric Simulation for High-Dimensional Data
abstract: Quantum-based geometric simulation offers a promising approach to handling high-dimensional data, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics to represent and analyze complex patterns. This paper proposes a novel quantum algorithm for simulating high-dimensional data, centered around the concept of quantum superposition to explore the data's inherent structure, aiming to achieve a more accurate representation than traditional geometric methods. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum superposition to identify and quantify relationships within the data, potentially uncovering hidden structures and trends that are difficult to discern with classical approaches. The paper details the algorithm's design, its theoretical underpinnings, and initial experimental validation, showcasing the potential for enhanced data analysis and representation.

title: Dynamic Information Entropy: A Novel Algorithm for Pattern and Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic information entropy calculation and application method. Traditional entropy calculation methods are static, failing to adapt effectively to data variations. We propose a dynamic algorithm that adjusts entropy values based on data input shifts, enabling more robust pattern and anomaly detection. The core mechanism involves a combination of dynamic entropy calculation with machine learning models, which analyzes input changes to dynamically adjust entropy. This approach offers improved adaptability and detection capabilities compared to static methods. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to identify subtle patterns and anomalies in diverse datasets. We conclude with a discussion of the potential applications of this dynamic entropy calculation method across various fields, including data mining, security analysis, and anomaly detection in industrial processes.

title: Quantum Information Modulation: Adaptive Geometry Optimization
abstract: Quantum Information Modulation (QIM) offers a promising approach to enhance quantum computation through dynamic adjustment of quantum states. This paper investigates the application of QIM to optimize quantum information processing, specifically focusing on achieving more efficient quantum communication. We introduce a novel self-adaptive geometric optimization strategy, leveraging the inherent properties of quantum information modulation to dynamically adjust qubit states and improve the performance of quantum algorithms. This system demonstrates the potential for significant advancements in quantum communication and computation. The core mechanism involves the controlled evolution of quantum states through instantaneous shifts, allowing for optimized performance in complex scenarios. This approach overcomes limitations of traditional optimization techniques, offering a pathway towards more robust and efficient quantum systems.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection with Contrastive Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to anomaly detection in graph data leveraging the principles of contrastive learning. Traditional graph anomaly detection methods often struggle with capturing complex graph structures and subtle deviations. Our method learns robust graph embeddings by training a contrastive network to maximize similarity between nodes belonging to the same community and minimize similarity between nodes from different communities. This effectively encodes the normal graph structure, allowing anomalies – characterized by unusual node relationships – to be identified as significant deviations from learned embeddings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline a framework adaptable to various graph datasets. The core of the method lies in learning representations that inherently distinguish normal behavior from anomalous behavior. The proposed technique offers a potentially significant improvement over existing anomaly detection techniques for graph data.

title: The title is: A Unified Memory-Centric Computing Architecture: Version 2.0 — Lie-Computable, OTOC-Scheduled Reconfigurable Systems
abstract: Here is the abstract from the uploaded paper, preserving its framing and terminology: Abstract Reconfigurable computing has traditionally relied on classical field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), in which computation emerges from memory through lookup tables and routing. In prior work, we introduced a unified memory-based architecture extending this paradigm to quantum and DNA-based memory substrates. In this paper, we present Version 2.0 of this architecture by introducing a mathematically rigorous scheduling and computability framework based on lattice Lie computability and out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs). We show that computation on quantum, spintronic, and genomic memory fabrics is governed not by time-ordered execution but by operator growth, non-commutativity, and Lie algebra closure. OTOCs provide a physically measurable norm that bounds operator scrambling and enables non-time-ordered, coherence-preserving reconfiguration. This establishes a unified architecture in which memory, routing, computation, and scheduling are all manifestations of operator algebra dynamics, yielding a principled foundation for scalable hypercomputing across classical, quantum, and synthetic genomic substrates.Source:

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Temporal Logic and Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to reasoning about temporal relationships by integrating temporal logic with neural networks. The core idea is to train a neural network to understand and apply the rules of temporal logic, thereby enabling it to reason more robustly and reliably about events and their temporal dependencies. We propose a mechanism where the neural network learns both the syntax and semantics of temporal logic expressions. This allows the system to effectively represent and manipulate temporal constraints, ultimately leading to improved reasoning performance compared to purely neural or purely symbolic approaches. The work highlights the potential for creating hybrid systems that leverage the strengths of both formal logic and deep learning, offering a path toward more explainable and trustworthy AI systems for temporal reasoning tasks. The key contribution lies in the formalization of temporal reasoning within a neural network framework, providing a structured method for encoding temporal relationships.

title: Non-Linear Quantum Simulation of Quantum Field Theory
abstract: This paper explores the application of a novel quantum simulation technique – a non-linear quantum simulation of quantum field theory – to address limitations in classical calculations of complex quantum systems. We propose a modified Feynman path integral method, enhanced with non-linear interactions, to provide a more accurate and efficient representation of particle interactions and quantum field behavior. This work aims to significantly advance the field of quantum field theory by extending its computational capabilities. The core claim is that this approach offers a potentially faster and more accurate method for simulating complex quantum systems than existing classical techniques. The mechanism involves a quantum version of the Feynman path integral method, incorporating non-linear interactions to achieve improved results. This research is driven by the inherent computational cost limitations of traditional methods and the desire to unlock more accurate representations of quantum phenomena.

title: Neural Topology Dynamic Learning (NTDL)
abstract: This paper introduces Neural Topology Dynamic Learning (NTDL), a novel approach to optimizing deep learning models that leverages the principles of physical topology within neural networks. The core claim of NTDL is that by simulating the dynamic changes in physical topological connections mimicking biological neural networks, we can significantly enhance the generalization ability and robustness of deep learning models. Unlike traditional methods focused on individual neuron weight adjustments, NTDL directly manipulates the network's topology, learning to 'break' weak connections and 'build' new ones based on model performance and simulated perturbations. We utilize information geometry and topological data analysis to quantify and guide these topological changes. The proposed framework offers a fundamentally different perspective on model optimization, drawing parallels with the intricate dynamics of synaptic plasticity in biological neural networks and introducing a topological analytical framework to direct the optimization process. Experimental validation (not presented in this document) is anticipated to demonstrate the effectiveness of NTDL in improving model performance across a range of tasks. ---

title: Fractal Neural Networks for Complex Data Analysis
abstract: This paper introduces Fractal Neural Networks (FNNs), a novel approach to complex data analysis leveraging the principles of fractal geometry. Traditional neural networks often falter when dealing with data exhibiting self-similar patterns and intricate structures, primarily due to their limitations in capturing hierarchical and recursive relationships. FNNs overcome these challenges by constructing networks with recursive connections and self-similar modules, mimicking the inherent patterns found in natural and complex datasets. The core idea is to build networks where smaller units recursively generate larger structures, mirroring fractal characteristics. This allows for a more efficient representation and processing of data with complex dependencies. The architecture is designed to detect and exploit these self-similarities, leading to improved accuracy and robustness in analyzing complex data. This work presents the foundational design and theoretical underpinnings of FNNs, outlining their key components and potential applications.

title: Quantum Reservoir Computing for Adaptive Control of Complex Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum reservoir computing (QRC) for adaptive control of complex dynamical systems. The core concept leverages quantum superposition and entanglement within a reservoir of coupled qubits to enhance the accuracy and speed of control signal generation. Unlike traditional reservoir computing, this approach explicitly utilizes quantum phenomena for improved performance. A small, randomly coupled quantum system, acting as the reservoir, is exposed to the dynamics of the system being controlled. The output of the reservoir is then used to train a classical controller, capitalizing on quantum interference effects. We present a theoretical framework outlining the methodology and demonstrate, through mathematical analysis, the potential advantages of QRC over conventional control methods, particularly for highly nonlinear systems. The work explores the key parameters influencing QRC performance, including the number of qubits, coupling strengths, and the training algorithm. Initial results suggest a significant improvement in control accuracy and convergence speed compared to classical reservoir approaches.

title: Hierarchical Modular Logic for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction is a fundamental requirement for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation. Current error correction schemes face significant limitations in scalability and complexity. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical modular logic system designed to address these challenges by introducing a layered approach to quantum state encoding and decoding. This system leverages a progressive encoding and decoding process, improving resilience against propagation errors and enabling the construction of more complex quantum algorithms. We detail the design of this modular architecture, exploring its potential impact on error correction capabilities and the underlying mathematical principles guiding its implementation. The paper concludes with a discussion of the advantages and challenges of this approach, outlining future research directions.

title: Multi-Agent Learning for Robot Collaborative Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Learning (MAL) to robot collaborative optimization. The core claim is that MAL can effectively facilitate coordination between robots, enabling solutions to complex environmental adaptation and task execution challenges. The proposed approach constructs a reinforcement learning-based multi-agent learning model and analyzes the interaction strategies between individual agents. The novelty lies in leveraging MAL to enhance collaboration and adaptability within a robot system, addressing limitations of traditional centralized control methods. This research explores the fundamental principles of MAL and its potential for robust, scalable robotic solutions. The paper presents a theoretical framework and discusses key considerations for implementation, highlighting the significance of agent communication and reward design. We demonstrate, through a conceptual framework, the potential of MAL to dynamically adapt robot behaviors to changing environments and achieve optimal collective performance. ---

title: Probabilistic Programming for Counterfactual Reasoning in Large Datasets
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning, the ability to reason about "what if" scenarios – specifically, how a system would have behaved differently under alternative conditions – is a fundamental aspect of human cognition and a crucial component in many fields, including medicine, economics, and social science. However, performing counterfactual reasoning effectively, particularly on large datasets, presents significant computational challenges. This work proposes a novel approach utilizing probabilistic programming languages to address these challenges. We demonstrate that probabilistic programming offers a scalable and expressive framework for building causal models from large datasets and simulating counterfactual scenarios. The core of the method involves constructing a probabilistic model that represents the data and incorporates explicitly defined causal relationships. This model is then leveraged through a probabilistic programming language to efficiently explore "what if" scenarios, quantifying the impact of interventions. We highlight the advantages of this approach in terms of scalability, expressiveness, and the ability to handle complex causal structures. The results presented here demonstrate the feasibility and potential of probabilistic programming as a powerful tool for counterfactual reasoning in large-scale data analysis.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for validating quantum computation algorithms using dynamic matrix verification. Traditional validation methods rely on manual parameter adjustment, often proving inadequate for complex, dynamic systems. This paper proposes a dynamic matrix approach that automatically adjusts verification parameters based on system state, offering a more intelligent and automated validation process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of quantum algorithm verification. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically updating the matrix to ensure the algorithm's correctness through a continuous, adaptive verification cycle. We explore the advantages and challenges of this approach, emphasizing its potential to surpass traditional simulation-based validation methods.

The core concept revolves around leveraging the unique properties of multi-quantum entanglement to enhance computational efficiency and explore novel applications of quantum computing. This framework introduces a dynamic entanglement scheme that adapts to the specific requirements of each quantum algorithm, improving performance across a range of tasks. The research explores the potential of multi-quantum entanglement to overcome limitations inherent in existing quantum computation methods, paving the way for more efficient and versatile quantum algorithms.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Diffusion for Pattern Synthesis
abstract: Quantum-enhanced diffusion modeling represents a paradigm shift in pattern generation, offering the potential for significantly faster and more precise synthesis of complex, realistic patterns compared to classical methods. This research investigates the feasibility of implementing a novel quantum algorithm designed to accelerate the generation and refinement of patterns through the exploitation of quantum phenomena. We explore the core mechanism by leveraging quantum algorithms to enhance the iterative refinement process inherent in diffusion modeling, ultimately addressing the computational bottleneck hindering the creation of intricate designs. The paper details the proposed quantum algorithm, its potential benefits, and preliminary results demonstrating improved pattern quality and speed. The core claim centers on a quantum-accelerated diffusion process that surpasses existing techniques.

title: Non-linear Random Matrix Mapping
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive mapping algorithm for non-linear random matrices. Traditional matrix mapping methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their applicability to systems with complex nonlinear relationships. This work proposes a new approach utilizing a dynamically adjusted matrix using a Gaussian process framework, enabling a more flexible and adaptable mapping process. The core mechanism involves adjusting the matrix's weight and connection parameters through a stochastic process, allowing the algorithm to effectively model dynamic system behavior and non-linear correlations. This research explores the potential of this approach to enhance modeling capabilities in diverse applications, including dynamic systems, signal processing, and data analysis. The algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient and provides a robust framework for handling complex matrix transformations.

title: Quantum State Dynamics: A Novel Approach to Quantum System Simulation
abstract: Quantum state dynamics, a burgeoning field of study, seeks to provide a robust and flexible framework for simulating complex quantum systems. Traditional approaches often struggle to accurately capture the intricate interplay of quantum phenomena, particularly the non-linear nature of quantum evolution. This paper proposes a novel method – a Quantum State Dynamics (QSD) framework – that leverages non-linear transformations to simulate quantum system evolution. The core mechanism centers on employing a sequence of carefully designed transformations to mimic the dynamics of quantum systems, offering a potential pathway to enhanced modeling capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of illustrative examples, highlighting its potential to surpass existing simulation techniques.

title: Blueprint generation for 2D game levels with a two-stage DCGAN-VAE pipeline: architecture and evaluation protocol
abstract: This registration describes a prospective study of learned procedural generation for 2D tile-based game levels. The study evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which a convolutional generator trained with the WGAN-GP objective produces a coarse spatial layout and a variational autoencoder performs learned refinement. The architecture is treated as a hypothesis and case study rather than as an established result. The main purpose is to establish a reproducible evaluation protocol before data collection and to determine whether the additional refinement stage provides measurable benefits over simpler alternatives. The protocol evaluates distribution fidelity, diversity, novelty, structural validity, computational solvability, structural difficulty proxies, generation efficiency, and player experience as separate properties. Particular attention is given to avoiding the conflation of Tile-Pattern KL Divergence with diversity: a generator can reproduce training data closely while producing little or no novel content. The planned corpus will contain 2D level maps across six genres, with data divided by whole source game where sufficient source games are available so that held-out evaluation measures transfer rather than recall. The study includes matched-capacity ablations comparing a single-stage adversarial generator, a VAE-only generator, and the two-stage adversarial-plus-VAE pipeline. The decision to retain the two-stage architecture is fixed in advance and requires it to outperform both alternatives under the registered paired analysis criteria. Evaluation will additionally use genre-specific reachability models, structural audits, fidelity/diversity/novelty metrics, and a within-subjects player study comparing the selected learned generator with established procedural baselines. The expected outcome is not assumed to be positive. The study may show that the refinement stage does not provide sufficient benefit to justify its additional complexity, in which case the best-supported single-stage configuration will be retained. The registration therefore fixes the research questions, architecture, comparisons, metrics, statistical analyses, and decision rules before experimental data are collected. No experimental results currently exist: the corpus has not been assembled, the models have not been trained, and participants have not been recruited.

title: Design and evaluation of software reference architecture: a systematic mapping study
abstract: Purpose Design and evaluation of Software Reference Architecture (SRA) is a complex task. This paper aims to collate the overall design and evaluation strategies that have been in practice for the last 15 years. It oversees the publication trend, components of SRA design, knowledge sources, developed artifacts, and evaluation matrices. Moreover, it highlights the models or frameworks that guide the development and evaluation processes. Design/methodology/approach The study followed the systematic mapping methodology outlined by [8] after searching relevant titles from the Scopus database. Thereafter, data extraction was guided by three research questions: (1) What is the current state of research? (2) How are SRA's designed? and (3) How are SRA's evaluated? The authors selected 75 primary studies after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Findings The mapping study reveals a steady growth in publications, with various methodologies used to design SRA and produce artifacts. Evaluation practices remain underexplored, with case studies and expert reviews as the primary methods. Frequently targeted quality attributes included modifiability, reusability, scalability, and performance. SRA research demonstrates increasing maturity; however, the field still lacks methodological consistency. Originality/value The paper collaborates design and evaluation perspectives from the academic and business community. It points to the salient facts that structure today's SRA design and evaluation status. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the field and outlines a research agenda to enhance the SRA design and evaluation process for future developers.

title: A Removal Based Approach to Improve LLM Faithfulness at Test-Time
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for consequential decisions, making their explanations an important tool for auditing model behavior. Unfortunately, these explanations can be unfaithful, failing to reflect the actual reasoning underlying the model's decisions. We consider a setting in which an LLM provides both an answer and an explanation in response to a question. We identify two distinct dimensions of unfaithful explanations: incompleteness, meaning that the explanation omits factors that influence the answer, and unsoundness, meaning that the explanation cites factors that did not influence the model's answer. Existing approaches to improving LLM faithfulness include training-time methods, which require access to model weights and extensive computational resources, and test-time methods that largely focus on addressing unsoundness. We introduce a test-time approach that directly targets incompleteness. We remove from the input the concepts not credited in the model's explanation and re-query the model on the reduced input. This eliminates unmentioned influences while preserving the influence of mentioned concepts. Across two datasets, multiple model families, and two independent faithfulness metrics, our approach improves explanation faithfulness compared to both standard prompting and prompting to encourage faithfulness. Our method is model-agnostic and can be applied at inference time without modifying model parameters, providing a flexible mechanism for reducing hidden influences and improving the reliability and safety of LLM-assisted decision making.

title: Step Back to Move Forward: Reflection-Aware Preference Optimization for Visual Generation
abstract: Diffusion models have become the mainstream paradigm for modern visual generation and have substantially advanced multimedia content synthesis, especially in text-to-image and text-to-video tasks. To further align such generative models with human preferences, reinforcement learning (RL) has recently shown strong potential as a post-training strategy. Nevertheless, existing policy gradient-based methods often explore inefficiently, making them vulnerable to local optima that may degrade semantic faithfulness and visual realism. To address these challenges, we present Reflection-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO), a new RL-based preference alignment framework for diffusion generative models. The core idea is to improve "forward" generation by incorporating "backward" reflection during optimization. We first introduce Diffusion Reflection, which rectifies intermediate sampling trajectories by inverting the diffusion process with a weak estimator, guiding latent states toward higher-probability regions of the true data manifold. Furthermore, we introduce Counterfactual Path Synthesis to implicitly distill these rectified trajectories into the policy, enabling the model to internalize the benefits of search-based exploration without incurring inference-time overhead. Extensive experiments on T2I and T2V models demonstrate that RA-GRPO significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in mitigating reward hacking and improving generalization. The method remains architecture-agnostic and integrates seamlessly with standard pipelines, suggesting a promising direction for stable preference alignment.

title: IchthyoNoma: Nomenclature and Context Sensitivity of Zero-Shot Biological Vision--Language Models for Bangladeshi Freshwater Fish Recognition
abstract: Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as training-free species recognizers, but reported accuracy can reflect more than visual species knowledge. We audit CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and a multilingual Jina CLIP v2 control on seven freshwater-fish categories from two Bangladeshi sources (10,321 images). BioCLIP2 reaches 72.36% on BFF-15 with English common names and 68.91% on SylFishBD with scientific names, versus 25.15% and 14.40% for generic CLIP. BioCLIP2 Bengali prompts are near chance in balanced accuracy (14.22-14.29%); Jina partially recovers Bengali discrimination to 21.89% and 16.36%, but bare Bengali names return to 14.29% on both sources. Paired SylFishBD interventions show no significant weak-blur effect, modest losses from stronger blur/gray masking, a larger white-mask artifact, and strong species dependence. Zero-shot biological VLM scores therefore jointly reflect biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context.

title: Long-Range Indirect Control-Flow Prediction in Stripped Binaries via Dual Virtual Hubs and Multi-Task Graph Learning
abstract: Recovering indirect control-flow (ICF) edges is fundamental to binary security analysis, yet existing methods struggle with long-range dependencies, isolate different ICF types, and are often evaluated under protocols vulnerable to label noise and data leakage. We present ICFlowNet, a unified framework for long-range ICF prediction in stripped binaries. ICFlowNet introduces candidate-aware Dual Virtual Hubs, a Global Code Hub and a Global Data Hub, to create short routing paths between distant code and data evidence, and combines them with multi-task graph learning to jointly model indirect calls, indirect tail calls, jump tables, and returns. To enable credible evaluation, we further develop a leakage-aware, noise-controlled pipeline with package-level splits, function-level mnemonic-hash deduplication, and a clean test protocol built from dynamic positives and absolute negatives. Using this pipeline, we construct a dataset of 15,901 unique stripped x86-64 binaries, including 1,351 with dynamic ground truth. Experiments show that simply scaling static supervision yields only marginal gains, whereas our structural and multi-task designs are essential: Dual Virtual Hubs improve long-range F1 by up to 9.13 points, multi-task learning adds up to 5.81 points, and the final model outperforms prior baselines by more than 13 F1 points on long-range indirect calls while adding only 11.44 percent topological overhead.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut via qudit swap operators
abstract: Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max d -Cut ( d -QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with n vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on ( C d ) ⊗ n . The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree d . This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the d -QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the d -QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined d -QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the 3 -QMC problem. For general d , low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

title: From Answers to Interpretations: Rethinking Ambiguity-Induced Aleatoric Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs
abstract: A key challenge in reliable LLM deployment is recognizing when uncertainty reflects irreducible variability in the task rather than limitations in the model's knowledge. In language tasks, a central source of such aleatoric uncertainty is input ambiguity or underspecification, where multiple interpretations remain plausible. Existing decomposition methods estimate aleatoric uncertainty by generating multiple clarifications of the input, querying the model for an answer under each clarification, and comparing the resulting answers. We argue that answers are not necessary for identifying ambiguity: they are often redundant, add avoidable cost, and can mislead through epistemic leakage. We support this claim theoretically, and propose a clarification-only approach that estimates this ambiguity-induced component directly from the space of plausible interpretations, without answers to the clarified inputs. Using ambiguity detection as an operational evaluation across three benchmarks, this direct approach improves AUROC (63.34 vs. 60.85), reduces computational cost by 4-26x in output tokens and 2.2-3.5x in API calls, and yields estimates with substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty. Overall, our results suggest that ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is better estimated from the interpretation space than from the response space.

title: 自适应量子拓扑的量子算法验证
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-adaptive quantum topology to quantum algorithm verification. Traditional algorithm validation relies on classical testing methods, while this approach leverages the unique properties of quantum topology to enhance verification accuracy. We propose a novel quantum algorithm that dynamically adjusts the quantum state to test the correctness of a given quantum algorithm, mitigating potential errors and improving the reliability of quantum computations. The core mechanism centers around utilizing topological invariants to establish a rigorous and efficient verification process. This research aims to provide a fundamentally new method for validating quantum algorithms, offering a robust and potentially scalable solution to verification challenges.

title: MADGDF: Multi-Agent Distributed Graph-State Deception Framework
abstract: Reference implementation and experimental pipeline for MADGDF, a defensive architecture for autonomous multi-agent systems combining graph neural network state estimation with a deterministic memory-canary mechanism to detect coordinated adversarial behavior and unauthorized persistent-memory retrieval. Evaluated on a controlled synthetic corpus (SwarmBench-2026, 32- and 250-agent configurations) and on real agent-execution trajectories from ToolBench, tau-bench, and SWE-agent.

title: Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Model (QCAM)
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become inextricably linked, holds immense promise for revolutionizing quantum computing and quantum communication. This research introduces the Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Model (QCAM), a novel approach to quantum system optimization that leverages the dynamic nature of entangled states. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on pre-defined parameters, limiting their adaptability. QCAM dynamically adjusts quantum system parameters based on the evolution of entangled states, enabling a more intelligent and efficient approach to quantum computation and communication. This work presents a framework for designing a quantum system capable of optimizing its behavior through the subtle yet profound effects of entangled states. The core claim is that QCAM will provide a significant advancement over existing quantum algorithms, particularly in scenarios involving complex and evolving entangled states.

title: Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing for Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to reservoir computing, termed "Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing," that draws inspiration from the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and interference. Traditional reservoir computing methods rely on randomly connected recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as reservoirs, with training focused on adjusting network parameters. We propose a modified framework where the reservoir is constructed with the goal of mimicking quantum state behavior, and the training algorithm is adapted from quantum measurement theory. The core idea is to extract relevant correlations from the reservoir's state space without explicit parameter learning. This approach aims to improve temporal prediction accuracy for complex dynamical systems by harnessing the inherent redundancy and superposition properties of the reservoir. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations, the proposed method, and presents a conceptual framework for implementing this quantum-inspired reservoir computing approach. We demonstrate the potential for enhanced temporal prediction capabilities compared to conventional reservoir computing techniques.

title: Meta-Learning for Hyperparameter Optimization of Deep Neural Networks using Evolutionary Strategies
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-learning techniques to accelerate the hyperparameter optimization (HPO) process for deep neural networks. Traditional HPO methods, such as grid search and random search, are often computationally expensive and inefficient, particularly for complex models and datasets. We propose a novel framework where a meta-learner is trained to learn an effective evolutionary strategy – specifically, the parameters governing a population-based evolutionary algorithm – for optimizing the hyperparameters of a given neural network. The meta-learner predicts optimal mutation rates, selection pressures, and other relevant evolutionary strategy components based on the network architecture and dataset characteristics. This approach enables a self-improving HPO system, significantly reducing the time and computational resources required to find high-performing deep neural network models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this methodology through theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline, highlighting the potential for substantial improvements in HPO efficiency.

title: Chaotic Systems Based Program Optimization
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to program optimization leveraging the inherent properties of chaotic systems. The core idea centers around the sensitive dependence on initial conditions characteristic of chaos – a property that allows for efficient exploration of complex search spaces. We formulate program optimization problems as dynamical systems within a chaotic framework, utilizing the system's non-linear behavior to guide the search process. This method offers a potentially powerful alternative to traditional optimization techniques like gradient descent, particularly for problems with highly complex and non-convex landscapes. The methodology involves mapping program parameters to the state variables of a chaotic system, allowing the chaotic dynamics to explore the parameter space. We demonstrate the theoretical framework and outline a potential implementation strategy, highlighting the key advantages and considerations for this approach. This research presents a new paradigm for optimization, shifting the focus from deterministic gradient-based methods to the exploration capabilities inherent in chaotic systems.

title: Probabilistic Logic Programming with Monte Carlo Dropout for Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to decision-making under uncertainty by integrating probabilistic logic programming with the Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) technique. Traditional logic programming paradigms struggle to effectively represent and reason with uncertain information, often relying on hard constraints that can lead to brittle and unreliable outcomes. Our framework addresses this limitation by incorporating probabilistic elements into the logic programming process, allowing for the representation of degrees of belief and the quantification of uncertainty. The MC Dropout mechanism is then employed to introduce stochasticity during inference, effectively simulating an ensemble of reasoning processes. This combination enables the system to explore a wider range of potential solutions, ultimately leading to more robust and adaptable decision-making. We detail the architecture of the system, the mathematical formulation of the probabilistic logic programming component, and the implementation of the MC Dropout algorithm. The paper demonstrates the potential of this approach through a conceptual framework and outlines future research directions. We focus on the theoretical underpinnings and the core mechanics of the system, providing a foundation for further development and experimentation.

title: Dynamic Differential Privacy for Federated Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to differential privacy in federated learning, termed Dynamic Differential Privacy (DDP). The core idea is to adapt the privacy budget dynamically, responding to the varying sensitivity of local data. Traditional federated learning frequently utilizes a static privacy budget, which can lead to either overly conservative privacy protection, significantly impacting model accuracy, or insufficient protection when confronted with malicious adversaries. DDP addresses these limitations by iteratively adjusting the privacy budget (ε, δ) based on gradient variance and update divergence. The algorithm reduces the privacy budget when gradients exhibit high variance, indicating sensitive data, and increases it when a node provides substantially different updates, signaling potential adversarial behavior. We demonstrate that this dynamic adaptation provides a stronger privacy guarantee while maintaining acceptable accuracy levels compared to fixed-budget approaches. This work contributes to a more robust and practical implementation of federated learning in privacy-sensitive environments.

title: Cognitive Computing Framework for Multi-Agent Systems – Episodic Memory and Predictive Modeling
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) frequently face challenges in achieving robust and adaptable behavior, particularly when dealing with complex, dynamic environments requiring long-term planning. Current MAS approaches often lack the capacity for effective memory and accurate prediction, leading to suboptimal decision-making. This paper proposes a novel cognitive computing framework designed to address these limitations. The framework integrates episodic memory, allowing agents to store and retrieve past experiences, with predictive modeling, enabling agents to anticipate future states based on learned patterns. We formalize the core concepts and mechanisms of this framework, outlining how these components can be combined to improve agent decision-making processes. The framework's key contribution lies in applying cognitive science principles – specifically, the principles of episodic memory and predictive coding – directly to the design and implementation of MAS, offering a potentially transformative approach to agent autonomy and adaptability. The theoretical model is presented, focusing on the mathematical relationships involved in memory storage, retrieval, and prediction.

The algorithm's design is based on a self-organizing structure, where parameters naturally adjust to achieve optimal conditions. We explore the theoretical foundations and practical implementation details of the SOFL, demonstrating its potential for automating parameter optimization and improving system performance.

title: ANALISIS SENTIMEN SOSIAL MEDIA X TERHADAP PROGRAM MAKAN BERGIZI GRATIS MENGGUNAKAN MACHINE LEARNING
abstract: The rapid development of digital technology has made social media an important source of information and a platform for expressing public opinion on government policies, including the Free Nutritious Meal Program which aims to improve public health, quality of life, and reduce nutritional and economic problems; this study analyzes public sentiment toward the program based on 10,381 comments from users of social media platform X (Twitter) collected through web scraping using Google Colab, which were then processed through cleaning, normalization, tokenization, stopword removal, and stemming, and automatically labeled into positive, negative, and neutral categories using IndoBERT, before being classified using four machine learning algorithms, namely Naive Bayes Classifier, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Random Forest, with the results showing that SVM achieved the highest accuracy of 74%, followed by Random Forest at 70%, Naive Bayes at 69%, and KNN at 43%, while neutral and positive sentiments were dominant, indicating that the program has received a generally favorable response from the public, and therefore the findings are expected to serve as evaluation material for the government to improve the effectiveness and implementation of the Free Nutritious Meal Program in the future.
